title: City Scan Technical Reference
text:
Welcome
The City Scan is a diagnostic tool designed to equip cities with the early insights needed to address risk by:

Providing a rapid, data-driven snapshot of a city’s demographic, economic, climate, and risk landscape.
Leveraging remote sensing and geospatial analysis of any city in the world, using global datasets.
Revealing the interaction between the urban built and natural environments.


In this technical reference
This reference book is a structured technical documentation to use and operate City Scan as a diagnostic tool. Here, you will find documentations on City Scan overview, getting started, running a City Scan, tasks and data layers, repository structure, case studies & galleries, as well as contributing guides.


About City Resilience Program (CRP)
The City Resilience Program is housed within the Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery (GFDRR) at the World Bank.
To learn more about CRP and GFDRR visit our website.

title: 1  What is City Scan?
text:
1.1 What can the City Scan tell me?
This City Scan is intended to support operational teams in building dialogue around a city’s most pressing resilience challenges. It is designed as a conversation starter rather than a specific decision making tool. Thinking spatially about how urbanization affects the resilience of various urban forces, networks, and people helps equip officials to develop risk informed investment proposals, identify opportunities and barriers to unlocking private capital, and prioritize and coordinate future investments.

title: 1  What is City Scan?
text:
1.3 Why invest in urban resilience
Investing in urban resilience boosts long-term economic, social, and physical sustainability by safeguarding the gains from current developments for future generations. Greater urban resilience builds the capacity of local governments to help households, communities, and enterprises manage and avoid shocks and stresses, for example by damage-proofing infrastructure before a disaster or maintaining critical services afterward. This approach represents a significant shift from prior development trends, which concentrated investments on post-disaster reconstruction and recovery.






Note



For a hands-on introduction, see Running Your First City Scan.

title: 3  General Workflow
text:
3.3 Part 3. Running a Scan
When running a scan, we are essentially going through several phases. The general flow is collect → analyze → multianalysis → render.

Collect stage is retrieveing specified datasets as indicated in inputs configuration from various publicly available sources for the specified AOI. As an output, you will retrieve TIFFs, GeoJSONs, or Geopackages in your output folder.
To conduct collect stage, run in your terminal
scan --collect
Analyze stage is conducting various analysis on a single task, such as seeing the statistical distribution, applying threshold, extracting median/mean values, etc. As an output, you will retrieve various CSVs in your output folder.
To conduct analyze stage, run in your terminal
scan --analyze
Alternatively, you can batch data collection and data analysis together by looping over tasks by running:
scan --all
Or, you can leverage your computer memory and parallelizing data collection and data analysis together per tasks by running:
scan --all --parallel







Warning



[Internal Note] Perhaps in the future, scan --all and scan --all --parallel should be reserved to orchestrate the whole process, including multianalysis, render, and scan-calculations



Multianalysis stage is performing cross-task analysis after single tasks analysis have been executed. For example, this stage executes analysis of flood-exposed population, which requires both flood analysis and population analysis to have been conducted. To do this, run in your terminal:
scan --multianalysis
Render stage is generating various visualizations as results of previous stages. This includes rendering maps and charts as PNGs or HTMLs.
# Static maps — applies styling from source/layers.yml, writes PNGs to 03-render-output/maps/
scan --render maps
# Charts for a specific task — writes HTML to tasks/{name}/charts/index.html
scan --render charts elevation
To generate a compiled interactive quarto document and HTML of all tasks, run:
scan --render scan-calculations

title: 4  Setup Instructions
text:
4.2 Step 2 — Git
Git is a version control system that tracks changes and enables collaboration through GitHub. It is required to clone the repository and stay up to date with changes.
Git is pre-installed on most macOS and Linux systems. Verify with:
git --version
If not installed, follow the GitHub Git installation guide. Windows users can use Git for Windows.

title: 4  Setup Instructions
text:
4.3 Step 3 — Clone the Repository
git clone https://github.com/cityresilience/city-scan
cd city-scan

# switch to unified branch
git switch unified
All subsequent steps assume you are inside the city-scan/ directory.

title: 4  Setup Instructions
text:
4.4 Step 4 — Python Environment
City Scan requires Python 3.11. Choose one of the two options below.

4.4.1 Option A: Conda (Recommended — Mac, Windows, Linux)

4A-1. Install Anaconda
Download and install from anaconda.com/download. Accept the default settings and restart your terminal after installation.
Verify:
conda --version






Tipconda: command not found after install?





Conda was installed but not initialized for your shell. Run the appropriate command once:
conda init zsh        # macOS / Linux with zsh (default on modern macOS)
conda init bash       # Linux / older macOS / WSL
conda init powershell # Windows PowerShell
Close and reopen the terminal. You should see (base) in your prompt.





4A-2. Create and Activate the Environment
conda create -n cityscan python=3.11.8 -y
conda activate cityscan


4A-3. Install City Scan & requirements
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -e .
pip install -r requirements.txt


4A-4. Register Jupyter Kernel (Optional)
Only needed if you plan to use Jupyter notebooks:
python -m ipykernel install --user --name cityscan --display-name "Cityscan"




4.4.2 Option B: Bootstrap Script (Mac and Linux only)
Use this option if you prefer automated system setup or do not have Python installed.

4B-1. Run the Bootstrap Script
This installs Python 3.11.8 via pyenv and prepares your system:
bash bootstrap.sh






Note



Review bootstrap.sh before running. It installs system dependencies, pyenv, and Python 3.11.8, and updates your shell configuration. If pyenv is being installed for the first time, restart your terminal and run the script again.




4B-2. Run the Setup Script
Creates the virtual environment, installs dependencies, and registers the Jupyter kernel:
bash orchestrator.sh
When successful, you will see:

Python 3.11.8 ready via pyenv
A new virtual environment created
A Jupyter kernel registered: “Cityscan (Python 3.11)”

To activate the environment manually later:
source venv/bin/activate

title: 4  Setup Instructions
text:
4.5 Step 5 — R
R is used for maps, charts, and the scan-calculations report, and also for several data collection tasks (earthquake, Oxford, cyclones, flood events, GDP gridded, coastal erosion, sea level rise).
Download the latest stable R release (4.5.x or newer) from cran.r-project.org. The repo depends on a current ggplot2, terra, sf, and tidyterra stack that will not install cleanly on older R versions.
Verify:
R --version
R in VS Code: Install the R extension and, optionally, radian for a richer R console experience.






Note



RStudio works fine for R-specific work and can be downloaded from posit.co. For the full City Scan workflow (Python + R + terminal), VS Code is recommended.

title: 4  Setup Instructions
text:
4.6 Step 6 — Quarto
Quarto is the publishing system used to compile City Scan reports and the web visualization. It supports Python, R, JavaScript, and Julia in the same document.
Install from quarto.org/docs/get-started.
Verify:
quarto check

title: 4  Setup Instructions
text:
4.7 Step 7 — Google Cloud (gcloud)
City Scan uses Google Cloud for two services:

Google Earth Engine (GEE) — satellite imagery and geospatial analysis
Google Cloud Storage (GCS) — private data buckets (city-scan-global-data, city-scan-gcs-data)

If you do not yet have access to these resources, contact the project lead to be added to the Google Cloud project.

4.7.1 7-1. Install gcloud CLI
Download and install from cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install. After installation, initialize the SDK:
gcloud init
Verify:
gcloud --version


4.7.2 7-2. Authenticate
gcloud auth application-default login
This opens a browser window to complete the OAuth flow. Credentials are stored locally and picked up automatically by City Scan:

macOS / Linux: ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json
Windows: %APPDATA%\gcloud\application_default_credentials.json



4.7.3 7-3. Set GEE Project (Optional)
The default GEE project is city-scan-gee-test. To override:
export GEE_PROJECT=your-project-id


4.7.4 7-4. Verify Cloud Access
# Check GEE
python -c "import ee; ee.Initialize(); print('GEE OK')"

# Check GCS
gcloud storage ls gs://city-scan-global-public/ --limit=1


4.7.5 How Authentication Works in City Scan
Authentication is managed in core/config/:







File
Role




auth.py
Initializes GEE and GCS credentials


scan.py
Loads AOI, city config, and creates output folders


paths.py
Auto-detects input/output directories


gdal_auth.py
Configures GDAL for access to private GCS buckets via /vsigs/



Tasks that require GEE (forest, landcover, LST, NDVI, nightlight) or private GCS (WSF, fathom, landcover burn, basic info) are authenticated automatically. If authentication fails, those tasks are skipped with a warning.






Warning



Never commit credentials or JSON key files to the repository. Treat them like passwords.




4.7.6 Granting Access to a New Team Member

Go to IAM & Admin in the Google Cloud Console
Click Grant access
Enter the new user’s Gmail address under New principals
Assign the role Editor
Click Save

The new user then runs the following to authenticate locally:
gcloud auth login
gcloud auth application-default login


4.7.7 Troubleshooting







Symptom
Fix




GEE auth fails
Re-run gcloud auth application-default login


GCS 403 / 404 error
Confirm the account has the Storage Object Viewer role on the relevant bucket


“GCS credentials not found”
Check that ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json exists

4.8 Step 8 — Verify Setup
Run the built-in check from the repo root:
scan --check
This verifies that Python dependencies, R packages, Quarto, and cloud credentials are all in place. Fix any reported issues before running a scan.

title: 5  Inputs Configuration
text:
5.1 city_inputs.yml
The inputs/ folder controls everything about a scan: which city, which AOI, which tasks run, and the parameters for each task.
Three YAML files drive the pipeline:
Templates live in templates/. Copy them to inputs/ and edit before running.

title: 5  Inputs Configuration
text:
5.1.1 Identification








Key
Type
Description




city_name
string
Display name. Spaces and accents OK (Lobito Corridor, Lüderitz). Used for outputs, labels, and slugified scan_id.


AOI_shp_name
string (optional)
Stem of the AOI shapefile in inputs/AOI/ (no extension). If omitted, AOI is auto-detected from UCDB / OSM / 5km buffer around the city centroid.


prev_run_date
string YYYY-MM (optional)
Reuse a previous scan folder. Default: null (creates fresh mnt/{YYYY-MM}-{country}-{city}/).





5.1.2 Time ranges








Key
Type
Description




first_year
int
Start year for LST and time-series tasks. Sentinel-2 / Landsat data available from 2013-03-18.


last_year
int
End year for the same.


fwi_first_year
int
Start year for Fire Weather Index.


fwi_last_year
int
End year for FWI.


demographics_year
int (optional)
WorldPop R2025A year (2015–2030). Default: current year.





5.1.3 Accessibility (osm_query + isochrone)
OSM POI categories to fetch and walking-distance buffers for each.
osm_query:
  schools:
    amenity: [school, kindergarten, university, college]
  health:
    amenity: [clinic, hospital, health]
  police:
    amenity: [police]
  fire:
    amenity: [fire_station]

isochrone:  # meters
  schools: [800, 1600, 2400]
  health: [1000, 2000, 3000]

accessibility_buffer: 5   # % of AOI bounds to buffer for capturing amenities just outside the AOI


5.1.4 Flood (flood)
Drives the Fathom flood analysis.
flood:
  threshold: 15           # cm — minimum depth to count as flooded
  year: [2020, 2050, 2100]
  ssp: [2, 5]             # available: 1, 2, 3, 5
  return_period: [10, 100, 1000]   # available: 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000


5.1.5 Benchmarks (benchmark_*, bm_cities_*, nearby_countries)
Controls which cities to benchmark against for population/Oxford comparisons.








Key
Values
Description




benchmark_mode
sibling / oxford / auto (default)
sibling = only sibling scans; oxford = only Oxford auto-detect; auto = both.


bm_cities_manual
list of city names
Explicit benchmark cities. Resolved as sibling → Oxford → backup, in that order.


benchmark_backup
citypopulation / worldpop_ucdb / null
Fallback for manual cities not found as sibling or Oxford.


nearby_countries
pipe-separated country names
Filter for Oxford auto-detect (only relevant when mode includes Oxford).

title: 5  Inputs Configuration
text:
5.2 multi_inputs.yml
Same fields as city_inputs.yml plus the cities/multipolygon list. Two modes — use one (or combine, see below).

5.2.1 Mode A: per-city AOI folders
Each city has its own inputs/AOI/{city_name}/ folder with a .shp. Wards auto-detected from inputs/AOI/{city_name}_wards/ if present.
cities:
  - city_name: Windhoek
  - city_name: Swakopmund
  - city_name: Walvis Bay
  - city_name: Lüderitz
  - city_name: Aus
Per-city overrides supported:
cities:
  - city_name: Windhoek
    first_year: 2010      # overrides the shared first_year for this city only
  - city_name: Aus


5.2.2 Mode B: multipolygon file
A single vector file (GPKG, SHP, GeoJSON) where each row is a city. AOIs are auto-extracted to inputs/AOI/{city_slug}/.
multipolygon:
  file: inputs/AOI/lobito_corridor_cities.gpkg
  name_column: GC_UCN_MAI_2025


5.2.3 Mode B + filter
Combine multipolygon: with a cities: list to extract all AOIs but only run a subset.
multipolygon:
  file: inputs/AOI/lobito_corridor_cities.gpkg
  name_column: GC_UCN_MAI_2025

cities:
  - city_name: Sakania
  - city_name: Lukuni
If a name in cities: isn’t found in the multipolygon file, the run errors out.


5.2.4 Shared settings
All other city_inputs.yml keys (flood, accessibility, FWI, year ranges, benchmark_*) work identically here and apply to every city in the list.

title: 6  Running a Scan
text:
6.1 Running Tasks
Tasks are run from the city-scan directory or from within mnt/scan-id using the general form:
Each task is divided into steps defined by {FLAG}:

title: 6  Running a Scan
text:
Note



Activate the cityscan Python environment before running any scan commands.



scan {TASKNAME} {FLAG}






Note



What is a scan-id? It is an automatically generated string with the format yyyy-mm-country-city (e.g. 2026-02-malta-malta). It is good practice to always specify the scan-id explicitly when running scan commands.










Flag
What it does




--collect
Runs data collection; saves outputs to 02-process-outputs/spatial/ or /tabular/


--analyze
Runs data analysis; creates output CSVs in 02-process-outputs/tabular/


--all
Runs both --collect and --analyze for all tasks enabled in menu.yml


--multianalysis
Runs cross-task analysis (currently flood exposure)




6.1.1 Running All Tasks
To run all tasks enabled in menu.yml:
scan --all
This opens a Terminal UI (TUI) showing per-task progress and logs.
Behavior depends on where you run it from:

From city-scan/ root — initializes mnt/scan-id and copies all necessary folders
From inside mnt/scan-id — writes outputs into the local 02-process-outputs/

To target an existing scan by ID:
scan --all --parallel --scan-id 2026-02-malta-malta

text:
6.2 Multi-analysis
Some tasks have cross-task analysis scripts — for example, flood-exposure calculations that combine flood and WSF outputs. Run these after all individual tasks have completed:

title: 6  Running a Scan
text:
6.3 Rendering Maps and Charts
After data collection and analysis, generate visualizations using the --render flag.

6.3.1 Maps
Applies styling from source/layers.yml and writes PNGs to 03-render-output/maps/:
scan --render maps --scan-id 2026-02-malta-malta
Maps read spatial data from 02-process-output/spatial/.


6.3.2 Charts
Writes an HTML file to tasks/{name}/charts/index.html:
scan --render charts elevation --scan-id 2026-02-malta-malta
Charts read CSVs from 02-process-output/tabular/.


6.3.3 Scan Calculations Reference Sheet
The scan-calculations render reads sections.yml to determine section order, then assembles all per-task charts/index.qmd files into a single combined HTML report:
scan --render scan-calculations --scan-id 2026-02-malta-malta
The compiled report is saved to scan-calculations/scan-calculations.html.






Note



If scan_calculations: True is set in menu.yml, the scan-calculations folder is automatically copied to the city folder when running scan --all.
See scan-calculations/README.md for details.

title: 7  Running Multiple Cities
text:
7.1 Option A: Separate AOI Folders
While a single-city run processes one city at a time, the --multicity flag lets you queue a list of cities and run them sequentially from a shared configuration file. Setup is similar, but inputs are organized per city rather than in a flat folder.
There are two ways to provide city boundaries for a multi-city run. Both use the same inputs/multi_inputs.yml config file and the same scan --all --multicity command.
Best when you already have individual shapefiles per city.

title: 7  Running Multiple Cities
text:
7.1.1 Step 1. Create inputs/multi_inputs.yml
This file follows the same structure as city_inputs.yml, with a cities: list added at the top.
cities:
  - city_name: Windhoek
  - city_name: Swakopmund
  - city_name: Walvis Bay
  - city_name: Lüderitz
  - city_name: Aus

# Shared settings — same fields as city_inputs.yml
first_year: 2015
last_year: 2026

flood:
  threshold: 15
  year: [2020]
  return_period: [10, 100, 1000]

# ... accessibility, FWI, etc.
All settings outside the cities: list are shared across every city. You can override any shared setting for a specific city by adding it under that city’s entry:
cities:
  - city_name: Windhoek
    first_year: 2010    # overrides the shared first_year for Windhoek only
  - city_name: Aus


7.1.2 Step 2. Organize AOI files by city
Each city needs its own subfolder under inputs/AOI/. Place the shapefile and its companion files (.dbf, .prj, .shx) inside that subfolder:
inputs/AOI/
  Windhoek/
    Windhoek_geoboundaries.shp
    Windhoek_geoboundaries.dbf
    ...
  Swakopmund/
    Swakopmund.shp
    ...
  Walvis_Bay/
    walvis_buffer_hull_1000m.shp
    ...
If a city has ward boundaries, place them in a sibling folder named {city_name}_wards/:
inputs/AOI/
  Windhoek/
    Windhoek_geoboundaries.shp
    ...
  Windhoek_wards/
    Windhoek_wards_geoboundaries.shp
    ...
Wards are auto-detected — no extra configuration needed.


7.1.3 Step 3. Edit inputs/menu.yml
The same menu.yml is used for all cities. Enable or disable tasks there as usual.

title: 7  Running Multiple Cities
text:
7.2 Option B: Multipolygon File
Best when all city boundaries are already in a single vector file (GPKG, SHP, or GeoJSON), with one row per city. AOI shapefiles are extracted automatically from the file into inputs/AOI/{city_slug}/ — you don’t need to prepare them manually.

7.2.1 Step 1. Create inputs/multi_inputs.yml
Instead of organizing AOIs into subfolders, point to the multipolygon file and specify which column holds the city names:
multipolygon:
  file: inputs/AOI/lobito_corridor_cities.gpkg
  name_column: GC_UCN_MAI_2025

# Shared settings — same as Option A
first_year: 2015
last_year: 2026

flood:
  threshold: 15
  year: [2020]
  return_period: [10, 100, 1000]
By default, all cities in the file are processed. To run only a subset, add a cities: list — all AOIs are still extracted, but only the listed cities are scanned:
multipolygon:
  file: inputs/AOI/lobito_corridor_cities.gpkg
  name_column: GC_UCN_MAI_2025

cities:
  - city_name: Sakania
  - city_name: Lukuni






Note



If a city listed under cities: is not found in the multipolygon file, an error is raised.




7.2.2 Step 2. Edit inputs/menu.yml
Same as Option A — one shared menu.yml for all cities.

title: 7  Running Multiple Cities
text:
7.3 Running
scan --all --multicity
Cities are always processed sequentially. All other flags work as expected:
scan --all --multicity --parallel      # parallel tasks within each city
scan --all --multicity --collect       # collect step only, all cities
scan wsf fathom --multicity            # specific tasks for all cities
scan --all --multicity --upload        # upload to GCS after each task

# Render for all cities
scan --render maps --multicity 
scan --render scan-calculations --multicity






Note



--parallel applies to tasks within each city, not across cities. Cities themselves always run one at a time.

title: 7  Running Multiple Cities
text:
7.4 What Happens Under the Hood
For each city in the list, the scan runner:

Extracts the city’s AOI — either from a {city_name}/ subfolder in inputs/AOI/ (Option A) or from the multipolygon file (Option B, which writes shapefiles to inputs/AOI/{city_slug}/)
Auto-detects the .shp file inside that subfolder
Generates a city_inputs.yml combining shared settings, any city-specific overrides, the detected AOI_shp_name, and a bm_cities_manual list populated with the other cities
Writes that city_inputs.yml to inputs/ and runs scan as a subprocess
The normal single-city flow takes over: creates mnt/{scan_id}/, copies AOI and wards files flat into 01-user-input/, and runs the enabled tasks
Moves on to the next city

title: 7  Running Multiple Cities
text:
7.5 Output Structure
Each city produces its own self-contained folder under mnt/:
mnt/
  2026-04-namibia-windhoek/
  2026-04-namibia-swakopmund/
  2026-04-namibia-walvis_bay/
  2026-04-namibia-luderitz/
  2026-04-namibia-aus/
The bm_cities_manual field links each city to its siblings, enabling cross-city population comparisons in the worldpop analysis.

title: 8  Customizing Maps and Charts
text:
8.1 Part 1: Maps
City Scan produces two kinds of visual outputs: static map PNGs (one per data layer) and interactive HTML chart reports (one per task). Both are customizable without touching the core pipeline — maps through YAML config files, charts through Quarto documents.

title: 8  Customizing Maps and Charts
text:
8.1.1 How map rendering works
Running scan --render maps --scan-id {id} executes core/R/maps-static.R, which reads two config files and renders one PNG per layer into 03-render-output/maps/:

source/layers.yml — the global style library. Each entry defines a yaml_key (e.g. population) with its title, palette, breaks, and other visual settings.
tasks/{task}/maps.yml — per-task config. Declares which yaml_keys this task contributes, whether to aggregate raster pixels into hexbins, and whether custom R scripts are needed.

The renderer matches each yaml_key to a file in 02-process-output/spatial/ using the fuzzy_string pattern, then applies the style settings to produce the map.



8.1.2 Changing how a layer looks — source/layers.yml
This is the file to edit when you want to change colors, legend labels, title text, or binning for any existing layer.
Each entry is keyed by a short identifier (the yaml_key) that the rest of the system uses to refer to that layer:
population:
  fuzzy_string: (?<!dense_)population.tif$
  title: 'Population density'
  subtitle: 'Number of persons per 10,000 m<sup>2</sup>'
  palette: ['#ECEB72', '#8E3933']
  bins: 5
  basemap: 'satellite'
  group_id: Population density
The fields you are most likely to modify:







Field
What it controls




title
Main legend header


subtitle
Secondary legend text (supports HTML)


palette
List of hex colors from low to high value


bins
Number of equal-interval bins (alternative to explicit breaks)


breaks
Explicit cut points including limits; for categorical maps, the factor levels


labels
Human-readable label for each bin (must match the number of intervals)


oob
Out-of-bounds handling — censor clips values outside the range


suffix
Unit string appended to legend values (e.g. °C, %)


factor: TRUE
Forces categorical (discrete) rendering



Example: Change the flood return period labels from short codes to plain English:
fluvial:
  title: 'Fluvial flood return period'
  labels: ['1-in-1,000 year', '1-in-100 year', '1-in-10 year']
  palette: ['#A7BCEE', '#1B35C4']
  breaks: [0, .11, 1.1, 10.1]






Note



The fuzzy_string field is a regex used to find the data file in 02-process-output/spatial/. Only change it if the task’s output filename has changed.





8.1.3 Changing which layers a task renders — tasks/{task}/maps.yml
Each task folder contains a maps.yml that tells the renderer what to do with that task’s outputs. The simplest form is just a list of yaml_keys:
# tasks/slope/maps.yml
layers:
  - slope
More options are available when you need aggregation, dependencies, or custom scripts:







Field
What it does




layers:
List of yaml_keys this task contributes (must exist in layers.yml)


aggregate_fun:
How to aggregate raster pixels per cell — mean, sum, median, min, max


aggregate_mode:
Aggregation grid type — hexbin, resample, h3, or none


aggregate_size:
Target cell size in meters


smoothing:
Pre-smoothing before rendering — method: gaussian/median/modal, window:, sigma:


depends:
Other tasks whose layers must be rendered too (used by custom scripts)


custom:
List of R script paths (from repo root) for non-standard maps



Aggregation example — population rendered as summed hexbins:
# tasks/worldpop/maps.yml
layers:
  - population
aggregate_fun: sum
Dependencies and custom scripts — flood maps that need built-up and population overlays:
# tasks/fathom/maps.yml
layers:
  - fluvial
  - pluvial
  - coastal
  - combined_flooding
depends:
  - worldpop
  - wsf
  - accessibility
custom:
  - core/R/map-flooding.R
The depends: entries ensure that those tasks’ standard layers are also rendered (so the custom script can read them). The custom: script then reads from spatial_dir and assembles whatever composite map it needs.



8.1.4 Adding a custom map script
Use a custom script when the standard pipeline — one raster, one style — isn’t enough. Common cases: overlaying two data sources, combining flood layers with a built-up hatch, or rendering a temporal sequence.
Pattern:
# core/R/map-deforestation.R
forest <- fuzzy_read(spatial_dir, "forest_cover")
deforest <- fuzzy_read(spatial_dir, "deforestation")

p <- plot_static_layer(data = deforest, yaml_key = "deforest",
  plot_aoi = TRUE, plot_wards = !is.null(wards)) +
  geom_spatraster(data = forest, fill = "#8CC056", alpha = 0.5)

save_plot(p, filename = "forest_deforest.png", directory = styled_maps_dir)
Key functions available (loaded by maps-static.R):

fuzzy_read(dir, pattern) — find and read a file by partial name or regex
plot_static_layer(data, yaml_key, ...) — create a styled ggplot using layers.yml settings
save_plot(plot, filename, directory) — save with consistent legend layout and dimensions
add_builtup_hatch(plot, underlay = FALSE) — overlay a 2025 built-up area hatch pattern; set underlay = TRUE to place it beneath point layers

Hook the script into the task by adding it to maps.yml:
# tasks/forest/maps.yml
layers:
  - forest
  - deforest
custom:
  - core/R/map-deforestation.R
To render only this task’s maps without re-rendering everything:
scan forest --render maps --scan-id 2026-04-namibia-windhoek

title: 8  Customizing Maps and Charts
text:
8.2 Part 2: Charts

8.2.1 How chart rendering works
Each task can have a charts/ folder containing a Quarto document. Running:
scan --render charts {task} --scan-id {id}
renders tasks/{task}/charts/index.qmd into an HTML file. All chart files across tasks are then assembled into a single combined report by:
scan --render scan-calculations --scan-id {id}
The order of tasks in that report is controlled by scan-calculations/sections.yml.



8.2.2 File structure
A chart folder needs two files:
tasks/{task}/charts/
  index.qmd      # the chart document
  _quarto.yml    # Quarto project config — copy from any other task
The _quarto.yml is nearly identical across all tasks:
project:
  type: default
  render:
    - index.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: [default, ../../../source/pagedtable-fix.scss]
Copy this from an existing task and change nothing. The pagedtable-fix.scss file applies Bootstrap 5 table styling fixes automatically.



8.2.3 Anatomy of a chart document
Every index.qmd has the same four parts. Here is the elevation chart broken down piece by piece.
1. YAML frontmatter
---
df-print: paged
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---
df-print: paged enables print_paged_df() for interactive HTML tables. The execute options suppress code, warnings, and messages from appearing in the rendered output.
2. Section header
## Elevation
Each chart section starts with a ## header. This becomes the section title in the combined scan-calculations report, so keep it short and descriptive.
3. Setup chunk (hidden, runs once)
#| label: setup-elevation
#| include: false
if (file.exists("_quarto.yml")) here::i_am("tasks/elevation/charts/index.qmd")
if (!exists("aoi")) {
  USE_GCS <<- FALSE
  source(here::here("core/R/setup.R"))
}
here::i_am() anchors the project root so here() resolves correctly when rendering from inside the charts/ folder — without it, here() points to the charts folder instead of the city root. The source(setup.R) call loads all libraries and creates the shared objects listed in the table below. The if (!exists("aoi")) guard prevents re-running setup when rendering via scan-calculations, which sources this file into an already-loaded session.
4. Data-loading chunk (hidden)
#| label: data-loading-elevation
#| include: false
elevation <- tryCatch({
  read_csv(str_subset(list.files(tabular_dir, full = T), "elevation.csv"),
           col_types = "cd") %>%
    rename(Bin = 1, Count = 2) %>%
    filter(!is.na(Bin), Count > 0) %>%
    mutate(percent = Count / sum(Count),
           Bin = factor(Bin, levels = Bin))
}, error = function(e) { message("elevation not available: ", e$message); NULL })
Wrap all data loading in tryCatch — if the CSV doesn’t exist yet, the variable is set to NULL and the chart section is skipped gracefully rather than crashing the render. Note the explicit factor(..., levels = Bin) call: factor levels are lost in CSV round-trips and must be restored after reading.
5. Chart chunk
#| label: elevation-chart
#| results: asis
if (is.null(elevation) || nrow(elevation) == 0) {
  print_text(paste_bold("No elevation data available"))
} else {
  elevation_plot <- ggdonut(elevation, "Bin", "percent",
    colors = c("#F2D7D3", "#DCBAC5", "#C59FB8", "#AF84A9", "#97679C"))

  print(elevation_plot)
  cat("\n\n")

  print_paged_df(elevation)
}
Always guard against empty data before plotting. Use plain print() for ggplots — ggplot2 >= 4.0 removed :::print.ggplot(). The cat("\n\n") after print() is required to prevent subsequent text from rendering beside the plot. print_paged_df() renders a paginated HTML table.



8.2.4 Objects available in chart documents
After source(setup.R) runs, these objects are available in every chart:







Object
Contents




tabular_dir
Path to 02-process-output/tabular/ — read CSVs from here


spatial_dir
Path to 02-process-output/spatial/ — read shapefiles/rasters from here


city_params
Parsed city_inputs.yml as a list


city
City name, title case


country
Country name, title case


aoi
City boundary as a SpatVector (EPSG:4326)


wards
Wards boundary, or NULL if not present


layer_params
Parsed source/layers.yml — use for palettes/breaks in charts






8.2.5 Adding a new section to an existing chart
Open the task’s index.qmd and add a new ## section following the same pattern:

Load the CSV from tabular_dir in a hidden chunk with a tryCatch guard
Add a ## Section Title header
Build the ggplot in a results: asis chunk
Call print(plot), then cat("\n\n"), then print_paged_df(df) if a table is also needed




8.2.6 Creating a chart for a new task

Create tasks/{task}/charts/
Copy _quarto.yml from any existing task (e.g. tasks/solar/charts/_quarto.yml)
Create index.qmd using the boilerplate structure above — adjust the here::i_am() path and the CSV filename
Render to check output:
scan --render charts {task} --scan-id {id}
To include this task in the combined scan-calculations report, add it to scan-calculations/sections.yml in the appropriate position

title: 10  Tasks & Structure Overview
text:
10.1 The City Scan Structure
City Scan is a standardized analytical framework for rapidly generating multi-thematic profiles of cities. Each scan draws on globally available geospatial datasets — satellite imagery, open administrative records, gridded models, and remote APIs — to produce a consistent set of maps, charts, and summary statistics across five thematic domains: population and demographics, economic activity, built form, climate conditions, and risk identification.
The pipeline is organized into discrete tasks, each responsible for a single dataset: downloading, clipping to the city’s area of interest (AOI), processing, and writing standardized outputs to mnt/{scan-id}/02-process-output/ (spatial and tabular data) and 03-render-output/ (maps and charts). Tasks are run independently and share outputs only through well-defined file naming conventions. This design means individual tasks can be updated, replaced, or skipped without affecting unrelated outputs.
This section provides a navigable overview of the documentation. Each chapter below corresponds to a thematic module; each listed item links to its documentation section covering what the layer is, why it is used, how it is produced, and the specific task scripts and output files involved.

What is it?
An annual city-level population time series from the Oxford Economics Global Cities Database, covering 2000–2040 (historical actuals through ~2021, projections thereafter). A companion chart shows the same series for a set of user-specified benchmark cities, enabling regional comparisons.
Why use it?
Population figures are typically used as a denominator for many indicators and as a measure of demand for services. High growth of urban populations — driven by natural increase, rural-to-urban migration, and the absorption of surrounding settlements — puts pressure on cities to meet demand for housing, infrastructure, and public services. Tracking growth relative to benchmark cities provides context for whether the city’s trajectory is typical for its region or income level.
How is this made?
Oxford Economics harmonizes data from national statistics offices, censuses, and administrative sources to consistent city boundary definitions. Year-over-year population growth percentages are computed from the raw time series.
How should we interpret it?
A consistently rising line indicates ongoing demographic pressure. Slowing growth rates can reflect urban maturation, suburbanization, or aging. Benchmark comparisons help identify whether observed trends are local or regional patterns.
Under the hood
The tasks/oxford/ task reads the Oxford Economics Global Cities Data CSV from a GCS bucket, filters for the target city and a set of benchmark cities, and produces tabular outputs covering population, employment, GDP, and demographic structure. The collection step runs entirely in R via tasks/oxford/collection.R. For population specifically, the pipeline produces _oxford_pop_growth.csv (population + year-over-year growth %) and _oxford_national_shares.csv (city’s share of national population, GDP, and employment in 2021).

What is it?
Annual population totals within the city’s AOI, derived from gridded WorldPop rasters. Two time series are shown: Global 1 (G1) covers 2000–2020 at 1km resolution; Global 2 (G2, R2025A) covers 2015–2030 at 100m resolution. Year-over-year growth percentages are computed from both archives.
Why use it?
Gridded population growth provides a spatially grounded complement to city-level estimates. Because WorldPop strictly clips to the provided AOI, these figures reflect population change within the administrative boundary rather than the broader functional urban area. The two archives overlap (2015–2020), allowing cross-validation, while G1 extends the record back to 2000 and G2 provides higher-resolution coverage and forward projections to 2030.
How is this made?
WorldPop G1 (2000–2020) tiles are downloaded directly from the WorldPop data portal at 1km resolution and mosaicked for multi-country AOIs. WorldPop G2 (2015–2030) tiles are downloaded at 100m resolution using the R2025A constrained model. For each archive, single-year rasters are stacked into a multi-band GeoTIFF and clipped to the AOI. Annual population totals are summed across all pixels; year-over-year growth percentages are then computed to produce the growth series shown in these charts.
How should we interpret it?
A consistently rising line indicates ongoing demographic pressure. Slowing growth rates can reflect urban maturation, suburbanization, or aging. Because WorldPop adheres strictly to the provided AOI boundary, population totals reflect only the area within that boundary and may differ substantially from broader metropolitan or functional urban area estimates.
Under the hood
tasks/worldpop/ downloads rasters from WorldPop directly or from a GCS mirror, handling multi-country AOIs by downloading each country tile and mosaicking with rasterio.merge. The _stack_mask() function stacks single-year files into a multi-band archive with band descriptions pop_{year}. clean_pg() in tasks/worldpop/analysis.py reads the stacked archive’s annual totals and computes year-over-year growth percentages. Growth charts are rendered in R via tasks/worldpop/charts/.

TipWhy does Oxford show a much larger population than WorldPop?





In the Oxford charts, Manila’s population exceeds 20 million, while the WorldPop charts show approximately 1.4 million. The difference is geographic scope, not data error. Oxford Economics uses Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) — for Manila, this corresponds to Metro Manila, which covers a large multi-city metropolitan region. The full FUA methodology is described here.
WorldPop analyses strictly clip to the provided AOI. When the AOI is the historic City of Manila (a single municipality), the population is approximately 1.4 million. The same WorldPop data for Metro Manila would produce a figure comparable to Oxford’s.

What is it?
A raster map showing estimated residential population counts at 100m resolution for the current year, clipped to the city AOI. Each pixel represents the estimated number of inhabitants within a 100m × 100m (10,000 m2) cell. High-density pixels correspond to urban cores and dense residential areas; pixels with zero population represent non-inhabited land.
Why use it?
Fine-resolution population density reveals where people actually live within the city — distinguishing dense urban cores, transitional peri-urban zones, and sparsely inhabited areas. Areas of high density signal demand for infrastructure, public services, and transportation; higher density also enables lower cost-per-capita service delivery. For resilience planning, dense areas concentrate exposure to environmental hazards, making density a key input for risk assessments and vulnerability mapping.
How is this made?
WorldPop uses a dasymetric disaggregation approach: census population totals from administrative units are redistributed into 100m grid cells using built-settlement layers derived from satellite imagery (the Built-Settlement Growth Model, BSGM). Pixels outside settled areas receive zero population. The population density map uses the Global 2 (R2025A) archive (2015–2030, 100m, constrained). The current-year band is extracted; if the current year falls outside 2015–2030, it is clamped to the nearest available year.
How should we interpret it?
High pixel values indicate densely settled areas such as urban cores and residential neighborhoods. Pixels with values ≤ 0 are masked as nodata, representing non-inhabited land (water, forests, agricultural land). Given the 100m resolution and modeled nature of the data, the map provides a high-level spatial overview rather than a census-precise count.
Under the hood
tasks/worldpop/ downloads rasters from WorldPop directly or from a GCS mirror, handling multi-country AOIs by downloading each country and mosaicking with rasterio.merge. The _stack_mask() function stacks single-year files into a multi-band archive with band descriptions pop_{year}. analysis.py:compute_stats() extracts percentiles, mean, sum, and count from the current-year raster. The population density map is rendered in R via core/R/ using the population layer definition in source/layers.yml. Charts (e.g., population time series) are produced in tasks/worldpop/charts/.

What is it?
A derived annual time series comparing population growth (%) to urban built area growth (%), producing a Population–Urban Growth Ratio. Values above 1 indicate that the city’s population is growing faster than its footprint — densification. Values below 1 indicate sprawl, where land consumption outpaces population growth. The series also includes population density (people per km² of urban area) for each year.
Why use it?
Cities that grow by expanding their footprint rather than increasing density tend to be less efficient in service delivery and infrastructure provision, and may signal unsustainable land consumption. Tracking the ratio over time helps planners understand whether growth is being absorbed through densification or through outward expansion.
How is this made?
WorldPop multi-year population totals (_pg.csv) and WSF harmonized urban built area totals (_wsf_harmonized.csv) are joined by year. Year-over-year growth percentages are calculated for both series independently, then divided. A density column (people per km²) is computed as population / urban built area.
How should we interpret it?
A ratio consistently above 1 indicates a densifying city with relatively stable or slowly growing urban land. A ratio below 1 suggests land is being developed faster than people are arriving — potentially low-density suburban expansion. Sharp changes in the ratio may reflect data gaps, boundary reclassifications, or rapid development episodes rather than true behavioral shifts.
Under the hood
This is a cross-task analysis. The clean_pug() function in tasks/worldpop/analysis.py reads _pg.csv (generated by clean_pg() from the WorldPop archive) and _wsf_harmonized.csv (from the wsf task). Both tasks must be run before this step produces a result. Division-by-zero cases (e.g., zero urban area in early years) are handled gracefully.

What is it?
A raster population dataset from the EU Joint Research Centre’s Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), providing population estimates at 100m resolution in 5-year snapshots from 1975 to 2030. This offers a longer historical window than WorldPop, making it suitable for multi-decadal trend analysis.
Why use it?
Understanding how a city’s inhabited footprint has evolved over 45+ years helps contextualize current density patterns and inform long-range growth projections. The long time series is particularly useful for identifying periods of rapid urbanization, post-conflict recovery, or population decline. As an independent dataset from WorldPop, it also serves as a cross-check.
How is this made?
GHS-POP redistributes population from censuses into 100m cells using the GHS-BUILT built-up surface layer as a spatial constraint — population is placed only within settled areas. The dataset is produced in the Mollweide equal-area projection (EPSG:54009) and reprojected to EPSG:4326 for City Scan use.
How should we interpret it?
Compare epochs (e.g., 1990 vs. 2020) to visualize where population has grown and which areas have remained sparsely settled. Minor discrepancies with WorldPop totals are expected, as the two datasets use different disaggregation methods and source censuses. The 5-year granularity means year-specific events are smoothed.
Under the hood
tasks/ghs_population/ loads a tile index shapefile (from GCS or the GHSL website as fallback), identifies intersecting tiles for the AOI, and downloads tile ZIPs in-memory. What is it?
Two complementary views of the city’s age-sex structure:

WorldPop demographics provides a spatially explicit snapshot — a 36-band raster (18 age groups × 2 sexes) at 100m resolution — that can be aggregated to produce an age pyramid, dependency ratios, and key demographic indicators.
Oxford Economics age structure provides a historical time series (2000–2021) showing how the share of Young (0–14), Working (15–64), and Elderly (65+) groups has evolved at the city level.

Why use it?
Age-sex structure is a fundamental input for urban planning: schools and pediatric services depend on child population shares; labor market assessments require working-age counts; elderly care infrastructure is driven by the 65+ share. Reproductive-age women (15–49) and youth (15–24) are tracked as distinct policy-relevant groups. Changes in structure over time — visible in the Oxford series — reveal whether a city is in demographic transition.
How is this made?
WorldPop R2025A age-sex rasters are downloaded as 36 separate bands covering ages 0–1, 1–4, and 5-year bins up to 80+, for both female (f) and male (m) categories. These are summed per band across all pixels to derive city-level counts. The 0–1 and 1–4 bands are merged into a single 0–4 group before calculating percentages. Dependency ratios are computed as:

Youth dependency ratio = pop(0–14) / pop(15–64) × 100
Elderly dependency ratio = pop(65+) / pop(15–64) × 100

Reproductive age is defined as 15–49. Working age is defined as 15–64.
How should we interpret it?
A bottom-heavy age pyramid (wider young cohorts) indicates high birth rates and growing future demand for schools and employment. A top-heavy pyramid indicates an aging population with rising demand for healthcare and elderly services. The Oxford time series reveals structural shifts — an expanding working-age share can signal a demographic dividend, while a shrinking one signals future pension and care pressures.
Under the hood
tasks/demographics/ downloads all 36 WorldPop rasters in parallel using ThreadPoolExecutor (3 workers). Each band is clipped to the AOI and stacked into a single multi-band GeoTIFF with band descriptions like f_0-1, m_5-9. analysis.py runs three sequential functions: demographic_aggregate() converts each band to a population count row; clean_pas() merges age groups, expands sex codes to full labels, and computes within-sex percentages; clean_adr() calculates youth, elderly, and total dependency ratios. Age distribution charts are produced in tasks/demographics/charts/ and the age-sex pyramid chart is rendered by core/R/chart-age-sex-distribution.R.

What is it?
A micro-estimate of relative wealth at approximately 2.4km resolution, covering nearly 100 low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The score is a z-score relative to the country’s national distribution — positive values indicate areas wealthier than the national average; negative values indicate poorer areas.
Two categorization schemes are provided:

City-relative (5 quantile bins): Ranks grid cells from “Least Wealthy” to “Most Wealthy” within the city. Useful for identifying intra-city inequality patterns.
Standardized (fixed SD breaks): Uses nationally anchored thresholds (< −1.0, −1.0–0, 0–1.0, > 1.0 SD). Useful for cross-city comparisons and understanding the city’s position within the national wealth distribution.

Why use it?
Relative wealth identifies spatial patterns of economic disparity that can guide targeted interventions — public investment prioritization, housing programs, and service delivery planning. Areas of concentrated poverty often have compounded vulnerability: lower access to services combined with higher exposure to environmental hazards.
How is this made?
The dataset was developed by Meta, based on Demographic and Health Surveys collected on the ground by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) from 66,819 villages across 56 low- and middle-income countries (LMICS). These surveys served as training data for a model using inputs that include satellite imagery, cellular network data, topography, and Facebook-connectivity data. The model was then used to estimate relative wealth in areas without recent Demographic and Health Surveys. The resulting value is the estimated average household wealth across all households in a given 2.4 km x 2.4 km area, in terms of standard deviations from the national mean. For more information, see the paper.
How should we interpret it?
For the standardized map, values near 0 are close to the national median; values above +1 are significantly wealthier and below −1 are significantly poorer than the national average. For the relative map, the five bins show intra-city distribution regardless of national standing — a city that is uniformly poor will still have a “Most Wealthy” bin, which refers only to the wealthiest areas within that city. Cross-region comparisons using only the relative map can therefore be misleading.
Under the hood
tasks/rwi/ downloads the country-level RWI CSV(s) from GCS, builds Point geometries from the lat/lon coordinates, projects to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), and estimates the grid spacing using the median nearest-neighbor distance among all points. Square polygons are constructed around each point using this half-spacing as a buffer. Two categorical columns are added: wealth_cat_en (5 quantile bins, city-relative) and wealth_cat_std (fixed SD breaks: < −1.0, −1.0–0, 0–1.0, > 1.0). The result is written as a GeoPackage. analysis.py computes per-bin area (reprojected to UTM for accuracy) and returns area-weighted histograms for both categorization schemes. Choropleth maps are rendered in R via core/R/ using the rwi_standardized and rwi_relative layer definitions in source/layers.yml. Distribution charts are produced in tasks/rwi/charts/.

What is it?
A map of cumulative nighttime light radiance aggregated over the most recent 10 years of VIIRS observations. Nighttime lights are a widely used proxy for economic activity: brighter areas indicate more artificial light from commercial, industrial, and residential activity. Higher values correspond to areas of greater sustained economic intensity.
Why use it?
Nighttime lights data is available globally and consistently, making it especially valuable in cities or regions where economic statistics are scarce or unreliable. VIIRS captures imagery at approximately 01:30 local time, which reduces interference from transient sources. Unlike aggregate GDP statistics, this dataset can be disaggregated to sub-city resolution, allowing identification of economically active neighborhoods — including informal economic activity not captured in official records.
How is this made?
VIIRS monthly composites are filtered to the most recent 10-year period using Google Earth Engine. Monthly avg_rad images are summed across all available months in the window, producing a single raster of cumulative nighttime radiance. The result is clipped to the AOI and exported at the dataset’s native scale (~464m).
How should we interpret it?
Areas of higher cumulative radiance should be interpreted as indicators of sustained economic activity, not a precise measure of output. Caveats apply: certain land uses (e.g., gas stations, airports, industrial zones) emit disproportionate light relative to their economic footprint, while daytime-oriented markets may show little nighttime signal. Use this map to identify spatial patterns and concentrate analysis rather than to read off absolute values.

What is it?
A map showing the direction and rate of change in nighttime radiance over the most recent 10 years. Positive values indicate locations where nighttime light intensity has been increasing over time — a signal of economic expansion or new development. Negative values indicate areas where radiance has declined.
Why use it?
Where economic activity is stable, the static radiance sum (Economic Hotspots) is sufficient. Economic Change adds a temporal dimension, revealing which parts of the city are growing, stagnating, or declining in economic intensity. This is useful for identifying emerging economic corridors, areas of disinvestment, or zones affected by major events such as industrial closures or conflict.
How is this made?
The same VIIRS monthly composite collection used for Economic Hotspots is used here. A linear regression is fitted to the time series of avg_rad values at each pixel, using the image timestamp as the independent variable via ee.Reducer.linearFit(). The resulting scale band — the slope of the trend line — is exported as the economic change raster.
How should we interpret it?
Strongly positive values indicate locations experiencing consistent growth in nighttime radiance, which may reflect new development, commercial expansion, or infrastructure investment. Strongly negative values may indicate economic decline, depopulation, or infrastructure damage. Values near zero represent stable or negligible change. The same caveats as Economic Hotspots apply: nighttime radiance is a proxy, not a direct measure of output.

What is it?
Two complementary gridded GDP datasets clipped to the city AOI: Total GDP at ~1km resolution (1990–2020, 5-year intervals) and GDP per capita at ~10km resolution (1990–2022). Both are PPP-adjusted in 2017 international dollars, enabling cross-country comparisons. The maps display the most recent available year: 2020 for total GDP and 2022 for per capita.
Why use it?
Gridded GDP enables spatial analysis of economic output within and around the city. Unlike aggregate national or regional statistics, the spatial resolution allows identification of economic concentration patterns, comparison of output across neighborhoods or districts, and overlay with hazard or population layers for risk-weighting. Having both total GDP and per capita values together supports analysis of economic density vs. efficiency.
How is this made?
The dataset employs machine learning algorithms trained on reported sub-national GDP data, achieving strong cross-validation performance (R²=0.79 for cross-validation, Pearson R=0.88 against reported data). Admin-2 level GDP per capita estimates are derived by downscaling from admin-1 level using ML, then multiplied by gridded population counts to produce total GDP at 30 arc-seconds. The per capita surface is retained at the native 5 arc-minute municipal-level resolution.
How should we interpret it?
High-value pixels indicate areas with concentrated economic activity or high income per capita. Pixels at 30 arc-seconds (~1km) blend multiple land uses, so values reflect sub-national area averages rather than building-level precision. In cities with strong urban-rural gradients, the urban core will typically appear as a distinct high-GDP cluster. GDP per capita at 10km resolution is most useful for regional comparisons rather than intra-city analysis.
Under the hood
tasks/gdp_gridded/collection.R reads two global GeoTIFF rasters from GCS using GDAL’s /vsicurl/ virtual file system and clips them to the AOI using the terra package. Total GDP values are converted from USD to million USD on export (gdp_tot / 1e6). Both outputs are multi-band rasters: one band per time step. Maps are rendered in R via core/R/ using the gdp_total and gdp_per_capita layer definitions in source/layers.yml, displaying the most recent band.

What is it?
Spatially distributed GDP maps broken down by economic sector — agriculture, industry, and services — at ~1km resolution for three reference years (2010, 2015, 2020). Each sector raster is produced by disaggregating sub-national GDP statistics using high-resolution land-use data from satellite imagery. A combined raster summing all three sectors is also generated.
Why use it?
Sectoral GDP maps reveal where different types of economic activity are concentrated within the city and its surroundings. Industrial areas, agricultural peripheries, and service-sector cores each have different profiles of flood exposure, employment density, and resilience. This spatial breakdown supports sector-specific risk assessment and business interruption estimation when overlaid with hazard data.
How is this made?
The SectGDP30 approach begins with country-level GDP decomposed into three sectors. Each sector is downscaled to a 30 arc-second grid in two steps: first via a population-based (PB) method that allocates GDP proportionally to population density, then reallocated to corresponding land-use fractions derived from satellite products (LUB method). The result shows strong consistency with sub-national statistics (R² > 0.9) and outperforms conventional population-only methods.
How should we interpret it?
High agricultural GDP pixels correspond to productive farmland near the city; high industrial GDP pixels indicate manufacturing zones or industrial estates; high service-sector GDP pixels align with commercial cores and dense urban areas. Comparing sector maps against population density or flood hazard layers reveals where critical economic activity is most exposed. Note that the service GDP map shows year 2015, as 2020 service data has coverage gaps in some regions.
Under the hood
tasks/gdp_sectoral/collection.py reads three global SectGDP30 rasters from GCS (one per sector per year) using rasterio. Each is clipped to the AOI, converted from million USD to thousand USD (× 1000), and written as a 3-band GeoTIFF with band descriptions gdp_{sector}_{year}. A combined raster summing all three sectors per year is then assembled; if a sector band is all-zero (data gap), the most recent non-empty year for that sector is substituted. Sector maps are rendered in R via core/R/ using definitions in source/layers.yml.

What is it?
Annual city-level time series of total GDP and GDP per capita from the Oxford Economics Global Cities Database, covering 2000–2040 (historical through ~2021, projections thereafter). GDP is reported in real US dollars at the functional urban area level. A companion chart places the city’s GDP per capita alongside benchmark cities for regional comparison.
Why use it?
City-level GDP and GDP per capita time series provide economic context that gridded rasters cannot: long historical trends, forward projections to 2040, and direct comparisons against benchmark cities at comparable points in their development. These indicators support assessment of whether the city’s economy is growing, at what pace, and how it compares to peers — a critical backdrop for infrastructure investment planning and resilience assessments.
How is this made?
Oxford Economics harmonizes data from national statistics offices, censuses, and administrative sources to consistent city boundary definitions. GDP is the aggregate measure of production equal to the sum of gross values added of all resident institutional units. GDP per capita is derived by dividing total GDP by population, and year-over-year growth percentages are computed from the raw time series.
How should we interpret it?
A rising GDP line indicates an expanding economy; a flattening or declining line signals stagnation or contraction. GDP per capita growth that outpaces population growth indicates rising living standards. Benchmark comparisons help identify whether observed trends are city-specific or reflect broader regional patterns. Note that Oxford uses Functional Urban Area definitions, so totals may differ substantially from those derived from smaller administrative boundaries.

What is it?
A breakdown of the city’s economic output by sector — consumer services, industry, financial and business services, transport and ICT, public services, and agriculture — expressed as shares of total gross value added (GVA) in 2021. GVA is the value of output less the value of intermediate consumption; it represents each sector’s contribution to total economic output. A companion chart shows the median sectoral shares for benchmark cities, enabling structural comparisons.
Why use it?
The sectoral composition of an economy determines its resilience profile and development trajectory. A city dominated by financial services has different vulnerabilities than one reliant on industry or agriculture. GVA shares reveal economic structure at a glance and support targeted resilience planning — for example, identifying which sectors drive employment and which are most exposed to specific hazards.
How is this made?
Oxford Economics estimates GVA by sector using a combination of reported city-level data (where available), downscaling from national or regional figures using population and employment location quotients, and productivity-adjusted employment data. City-center areas are weighted toward financial and business services; peripheries are weighted toward consumer services and industry. In developing countries without sub-national data, historical GVA growth in specific industries is additionally calibrated to population growth and inter-industry demand.
How should we interpret it?
A large consumer services share reflects a city that serves its own population (retail, food, hospitality). A large financial and business services share indicates a regional hub with high productivity. A sizable industry share may reflect manufacturing zones or resource processing. Comparing the city’s profile to the benchmark median helps identify structural similarities or outlier characteristics.
Under the hood
tasks/oxford/collection.R filters Oxford GVA indicators, computes sector shares as a percentage of total GVA, and saves _oxford_gva_sectors.csv (median shares for city and benchmark group) and _oxford_gva_sectors_individual.csv (individual city values). Sectoral shares reveal which industries drive livelihoods, and comparing against benchmarks highlights whether the city’s labor market is diversified or concentrated in sectors with higher climate or economic exposure.

Oxford Economics uses city-level employment statistics directly where available (covering Australia, Europe, Canada, the US, Mexico, and Brazil). Rapid employment growth alongside moderate population growth suggests rising labor force participation or in-migration of workers. A high share of consumer services typically reflects a service-oriented urban economy; a high industry share may indicate reliance on manufacturing that is sensitive to global supply chain disruptions. What is it?
The distribution of households across income bands (expressed in PPP constant 2015 USD), shown both as a snapshot for 2021 compared to benchmark cities and as a time series from 2002 to 2021 for the focus city. Income bands range from “Under $5K” to “Over $70K” per household. The area chart shows how the income distribution has shifted over time, revealing whether middle- and upper-income households have grown as a share of the total.
Why use it?
Household income distribution captures economic inequality at the city level and tracks changes in living standards over time. A growing share of middle-income households signals economic mobility and expanding consumer demand; a persistently large share of low-income households indicates structural poverty. Comparing the distribution against benchmark cities contextualizes whether observed patterns reflect the city’s specific conditions or broader regional income levels.
How is this made?
Household disposable income — defined as income from all sources (wages, interest, property, benefits, dividends) less taxes and social security contributions — is estimated at the city level. Where consumption and income data are unavailable, Oxford Economics estimates the city’s share of national disposable income using its share of national GDP and population growth, then derives private consumption through a savings equation that accounts for income-dependent savings rates.
How should we interpret it?
A shift in the area chart from lower to higher income bands over time indicates rising household prosperity. A dominant “Under $5K” band suggests a large population living near or below the poverty threshold in purchasing-power terms. When comparing with benchmark cities, note that PPP-adjusted figures remove the effect of local price differences, making cross-city comparisons more meaningful. These estimates reflect city-level averages; within-city inequality (e.g., wealthy enclaves vs. informal settlements) is not captured here — see the Relative Wealth section in the Population chapter for spatial inequality patterns.

What is it?
Three complementary views of when land was urbanized. WSF Evolution (1985–2015, 30m) provides the historical baseline, showing the year each pixel first became a settled area using Landsat imagery. WSF Tracker (2016–2025, 10m) extends the record into the present using Sentinel-2, at higher spatial resolution and 6-month temporal granularity. WSF Harmonized combines both sources into a single seamless 1985–2025 time series using a spatial backdating algorithm that reconciles the different resolutions and sensors.
The cumulative built-up area charts translate the raster data into a time series of total urban footprint (in km²), summarizing how quickly the city has grown over each period.
Why use it?
Understanding where and when urban expansion occurred has direct implications for infrastructure planning, service delivery, and resilience. Areas urbanized decades ago are likely to have older building stock and may have been built before modern land use or building codes. Rapid recent expansion may indicate informal settlement growth or peri-urban sprawl. The harmonized dataset’s 40-year continuous record enables analysis of long-term urbanization trajectories and changes in the rate of urban growth.
How is this made?
WSF Evolution was produced by the German Aerospace Center (DLR) using an iterative machine-learning approach trained on Landsat imagery, generating yearly settlement extents from 1985 to 2015. WSF Tracker uses Sentinel-2 at 10m with 6-month composites. The City Scan harmonization pipeline resamples the Tracker to 30m using modal resampling, identifies pixels that appear as 2016 settlements in the Tracker but are absent from the Evolution dataset, and uses Euclidean distance transform-based backdating to assign them plausible pre-2016 urbanization years from the nearest confirmed Evolution pixel. The remaining 2016-and-later pixels retain their Tracker year. Per-year cumulative built-up area statistics are computed in square kilometers.
How should we interpret it?
The maps display urbanization epochs in 5-year or 10-year ranges, revealing spatial-temporal patterns of growth. Areas shown as “Before 1986” on the Evolution map were already urbanized at the start of the record and represent the established historic core. Comparing Evolution and Tracker in the harmonized chart reveals whether the pace of urbanization has accelerated or slowed since 2016. Note that WSF does not track land that transitions back from urban to non-urban (rare but possible), and WSF Tracker tiles require private GCS access and may not be available in all deployment environments.
Under the hood
tasks/wsf/collection.py downloads 2-degree tiles: WSF Evolution tiles from DLR’s public GeoService, and WSF Tracker tiles from a private GCS bucket (/vsigs/city-scan-global-private/wsf_tracker). Tiles are merged and clipped to the AOI. For WSF Tracker, integer mode values are converted to fractional years (mode value i → year 2016.0 + i × 0.5). Harmonization is handled by harmonize_wsf() in tasks/wsf/analysis.py, which uses scipy.ndimage.distance_transform_edt for backdating and auto-calibrates the distance threshold at the 90th percentile of disputed-pixel distances. Cumulative area statistics are computed per year and source. Charts are rendered in R via tasks/wsf/charts/.

What is it?
A land cover classification of the city AOI at 10m resolution, derived from the ESA WorldCover v2.0 dataset for 2021. Each pixel is assigned one of 11 land cover classes: Tree cover, Shrubland, Grassland, Cropland, Built-up, Bare/sparse vegetation, Snow and ice, Permanent water bodies, Herbaceous wetland, Mangroves, and Moss and lichen. The companion donut chart shows the proportional area of each land cover class within the AOI.
Why use it?
Land cover composition reveals how the city’s territory is divided between urban, natural, agricultural, and water areas. Understanding these proportions supports sustainable planning — identifying opportunities to protect green corridors, expand urban greenery, or assess flood risk from impervious surface coverage. Land cover also serves as a cross-reference for WSF urbanized area estimates: built-up pixels from ESA WorldCover and WSF settle surfaces should broadly align, but differences arise from varying definitions of “urban.”
How is this made?
ESA WorldCover was produced by the European Space Agency using Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data, trained against the UN FAO Land Cover Classification System. The City Scan pipeline retrieves the ESA/WorldCover/v200 collection via Google Earth Engine, repins the raster to EPSG:3857 at 10m to preserve categorical pixel codes, and saves a clipped GeoTIFF. A post-processing step snaps any residual fractional values to the nearest valid ESA class code (10, 20, 30, …, 100).
How should we interpret it?
Built-up cover indicates the share of impervious or developed land, while tree cover and grassland reflect the extent of green and natural areas. A high built-up share with limited tree cover may indicate urban heat island risk. Cropland on the urban fringe signals agricultural land potentially under pressure from urbanization. Because ESA WorldCover is based on satellite reflectance signatures and not cadastral data, some misclassifications occur — dense shade trees may be confused with forest cover, and bare construction sites may be classified as bare soil rather than built-up.
Under the hood
tasks/landcover/collection.py fetches ESA/WorldCover/v200 from Google Earth Engine, reprojects to EPSG:3857 at 10m with nearest-neighbor resampling to preserve categorical values, and clips to the AOI. After export, pixel values are snapped to the valid ESA class code set. tasks/landcover/analysis.py reads the raster in blocks using windowed reads, counts pixels per class, and writes {city}_lc.csv. The land cover map is rendered in R via core/R/ using the land_cover layer definition in source/layers.yml. The composition chart is produced in tasks/landcover/charts/.

What is it?
A visualization of the city’s road network and a polar histogram (compass rose) showing the distribution of street bearings. Each bar in the orientation chart represents the proportion of street segments pointing in that compass direction, revealing the dominant orientations of the road grid. The road network map shows all OSM-mapped streets extracted for the city, buffered 5km beyond the AOI boundary.
Why use it?
Street network structure has long-term consequences for mobility, walkability, and urban resilience. A grid-dominated orientation provides route redundancy, shorter average travel distances, and more equitable access to destinations on foot or by vehicle. An organic, heterogeneous orientation reflects topography-driven or historically unplanned growth and may concentrate traffic on a limited set of routes. Understanding the road network structure informs infrastructure investment priorities, evacuation planning, and transport network resilience assessments.
How is this made?
The road network is extracted from OpenStreetMap using OSMnx with a 5km buffer around the AOI (network_type='all'). The graph is saved as both a GeoPackage (nodes and edges) and a GraphML file for fast reloading. Edge bearings are computed using ox.add_edge_bearings() on the undirected graph, and OSMnx’s plot_orientation() generates the compass rose. A road network map is produced via ox.plot_graph(). Major roads (primary, trunk, motorway, and their links) are filtered into a separate GeoPackage.
How should we interpret it?
Cities built with grid-based urban planning exhibit a clear cross pattern in the compass rose, with most street bearings clustered around two perpendicular axes (e.g., Manhattan). A circular distribution with no dominant orientation reflects organic urban form, where streets follow terrain, water, or historical paths rather than a planned grid. Intermediate patterns are common in cities where a historic organic core coexists with newer planned extensions. The network map also reveals gaps — areas with sparse coverage may indicate informal settlements not yet mapped in OSM, or zones with restricted access.
Under the hood
tasks/accessibility/collection.py downloads the graph via ox.graph_from_polygon(), buffering the AOI by 5km. The graph is saved as a GeoPackage and GraphML. Major roads are filtered from the edges layer using keywords (primary, trunk, motorway, etc.) in the highway attribute. The road network visualization is produced by network_plot() and the orientation chart by road_orientation(), both in tasks/accessibility/analysis.py. Network statistics (node count, edge count, average node degree, circuity, etc.) are computed using ox.stats.basic_stats() and saved to {city}_network_stats.csv.

What is it?
A raster map showing the density of road intersections per square kilometer, derived from the OSM road network. Each cell represents how many intersections fall within a surrounding 1km² kernel, revealing where the network is most connected and accessible.
Why use it?
Intersection density is a direct measure of street network connectivity. Dense intersection patterns indicate fine-grained grids with many route options, supporting walking, cycling, and vehicle movement. Low intersection density — typically associated with cul-de-sac suburban layouts or underserved areas — forces longer travel distances and reduces route choice. Higher intersection density is associated with more walkable neighborhoods, lower vehicle-miles traveled, and more efficient emergency response.
How is this made?
Intersection nodes are extracted from the OSM road network graph (nodes with degree > 2). These point features are passed to density_rast() in core/R/fns-geometry.R, which rasterizes the point density at 200 cells across the AOI extent and writes intersection-density.tif. The map is rendered in R via core/R/map-intersections.R using the intersections layer definition in source/layers.yml.
How should we interpret it?
High-density zones correspond to the urban core or grid-planned neighborhoods where streets connect frequently. Lower-density zones on the urban periphery or in areas with large blocks, highways, or industrial estates indicate reduced connectivity. Areas with very low or zero intersection density may represent inaccessible land uses (water bodies, parks, airports) or informal zones with limited mapped street coverage.
Under the hood
The intersection density raster is derived from the nodes GeoPackage produced by the accessibility task. core/R/pre-mapping.R reads the nodes layer, computes density using density_rast(), and writes intersection-density.tif to the spatial directory if it does not already exist.

What is it?
Network-based isochrone maps showing which parts of the city are within recommended travel distances of the nearest school and healthcare facility, measured along the actual road network. For schools, the analysis includes all OSM features tagged as school, kindergarten, college, or university. For healthcare, it includes all features tagged as health amenity, clinic, or hospital. Facility locations are displayed as point overlays.
Why use it?
Access to education and healthcare is a key dimension of urban equity. Areas beyond the recommended service radius — typically 800m for schools and 1km for healthcare facilities — may face service gaps that disadvantage residents who cannot travel far by foot or lack vehicle access. Mapping these gaps visually identifies underserved zones and supports prioritization of new facilities or transport improvements.
How is this made?
OSM POIs are extracted for each facility category using POI_collection() in tasks/accessibility/collection.py. The network-based isochrone analysis is performed by compute_accessibility_analysis() in tasks/accessibility/analysis.py, which calls make_isochrone() for each category. This function snaps each facility to the nearest road network node, computes shortest-path distances from all facility nodes to all other nodes using Dijkstra’s algorithm, then generates buffered isochrone polygons at configurable distance thresholds. Thresholds are set in inputs/city_inputs.yml under the isochrone key (e.g., [800, 1600, 2400] meters for schools and [1000, 2000, 3000] for health facilities).
How should we interpret it?
Areas inside the innermost isochrone are well-served; areas outside the outermost isochrone mark a clear service gap. Because the analysis uses the road network rather than straight-line distance, it reflects actual travel conditions. Note that OSM coverage is incomplete in many cities — particularly informal settlements — so the absence of mapped facilities does not necessarily confirm a service gap. The facility point maps provide a visual check on coverage.
Under the hood
POI collections are stored as {city}_osm_{key}.gpkg. Isochrone polygons are saved as {city}_{key}_isochrone.gpkg. Accessibility distances per node are merged into {city}_nodes_and_edges_accessibilities.gpkg for each category. Distance thresholds and the list of facility categories are fully configurable via inputs/city_inputs.yml. The isochrone maps are rendered in R via core/R/ using the school_zones, school_points, health_zones, and health_points layer definitions in source/layers.yml.
