tasks/solar/



What is it?
Solar PV potential is the estimated daily energy yield of a theoretical 1 kilowatt-peak (kWp) photovoltaic system, in kilowatt-hours per day (kWh/kWp). The annual raster shows the long-run mean yield across the city, while the seasonal chart shows how that yield varies month by month. Values above 4.5 kWh/kWp are considered excellent; values between 3.5 and 4.5 are favorable; values below 3.5 indicate below-favorable conditions.
Why use it?
Solar PV offers a pathway to long-term energy sustainability and resilience, especially in rapidly urbanizing cities where electricity demand is growing. Mapping spatial variation in solar potential helps identify optimal areas for rooftop or ground-mounted installations and supports planning for distributed renewable energy generation. The seasonal chart reveals how consistent the resource is throughout the year — consistent availability matters as much as peak yield for the viability of solar systems without battery storage.
How is this made?
The Global Solar Atlas 2.0 was developed by Solargis s.r.o. for the World Bank Group’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). It draws on long-term satellite observations (covering locations back to ~1994) to derive solar irradiance and photovoltaic output estimates using atmospheric models. The annual PVOUT raster represents the mean daily PV yield at optimal tilt under 100% system availability. A separate 12-band monthly raster captures seasonal variation across January–December.
How should we interpret it?
Within a city, spatial variation in solar potential is typically small — differences of 0.1–0.2 kWh/kWp across the AOI are common. In practice, PV siting decisions should weight other factors more heavily than the spatial distribution shown here: roof orientation, shading from adjacent buildings or trees, and ease of maintenance. The seasonal chart is more diagnostic — systems in places with high seasonal ratios (peak-to-trough above 2:1) may require storage or grid backup to remain effective year-round. The map alone should not be the primary basis for siting decisions; it provides a baseline potential, not a deployment plan.
Under the hood
tasks/solar/collection.py downloads PVOUT.tif (annual) and PVOUT-monthly.tif (12-band monthly) from the public GCS bucket and clips both to the AOI. compute_stats() in tasks/solar/analysis.py computes summary statistics from the annual raster and writes {city}_solar_stats.csv. plot_solar_seasonality() extracts per-band monthly means from the 12-band raster, writes {city}_solar_monthly_stats.csv, computes a seasonality interpretation (ratio of max to min monthly yield), and renders the seasonal availability chart. Area by PV condition bin (Less than Favorable / Favorable / Excellent) is written to {city}_pv_area.csv. The annual PV map is rendered in R via core/R/ using the solar layer definition in source/layers.yml.

What is it?
Three complementary views of the city’s PM2.5 air quality, all derived from the same multi-band raster:

Global scale map — PM2.5 concentration for 2022 using the WHO and US EPA standard breakpoints, enabling comparison against global health benchmarks.
Local scale map — same 2022 data re-classified into local quantile bins that emphasize intra-city variation.
Trend map — the linear trend slope in PM2.5 from 2013 to 2022 (µg/m³ per year), showing where air quality is improving or deteriorating.

PM2.5 particles (≤2.5 µm in diameter) penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream. Common sources include vehicle emissions, industrial combustion, biomass burning, and dust. The WHO guideline is 5 µg/m³ annual mean; the US EPA standard is 12 µg/m³.
Why use it?
Chronic exposure to elevated PM2.5 is associated with cardiovascular and respiratory disease and is a leading contributor to premature mortality in urban areas. Mapping PM2.5 concentration spatially identifies neighborhoods with disproportionate pollution burden and supports prioritization of emission reduction interventions. The trend map adds a temporal dimension — an improving trend (negative slope) signals progress; a worsening trend (positive slope) flags emerging public health risk.
How is this made?
Annual ground-level PM2.5 estimates are derived from satellite-retrieved aerosol optical depth (AOD) measured by MODIS, MISR, SeaWiFS, and VIIRS sensors, then converted to surface concentrations using geographically weighted regression (GWR) that accounts for spatial variation in the AOD-to-PM2.5 relationship. The City Scan pipeline downloads all 25 annual rasters (1998–2022), clips to the AOI, and produces three derived summary bands: mean_1998_2022 (long-run mean), mean_2013_2022 (most recent 10-year mean), and trend_2013_2022 (pixel-wise linear regression slope over 2013–2022).
How should we interpret it?
The global-scale map uses standard breakpoints, enabling direct comparison with health guidelines and other cities. Values consistently above 15–20 µg/m³ indicate a significant pollution burden. The local-scale map stretches the color range to the city’s own distribution, making intra-city spatial patterns easier to read — but values cannot be directly compared across cities using this map. The trend map is directional: negative values indicate improving air quality, positive values indicate worsening. Note that annual averages mask seasonal extremes — events like wildfire smoke or seasonal burning can produce concentrations far above the annual mean in specific months.
Under the hood
tasks/air_quality/collection.py downloads and clips 25 yearly PM2.5 GeoTIFFs from GCS (sdei-global-annual-gwr-pm2-5-modis-misr-seawifs-viirs-aod-v5-gl-04-{year}-geotiff.tif for 1998–2022) and stacks them into a single multi-band output. Three additional summary bands (mean_1998_2022, mean_2013_2022, trend_2013_2022) are prepended. Band descriptions are written to the GeoTIFF header. Maps are rendered in R via core/R/ using the air_quality, air_quality_local, and air_quality_trend layer definitions in source/layers.yml, each reading a different band from the same raster.

What is it?
Summer land surface temperature (LST) is the mean temperature of the ground surface — including soil, pavement, vegetation, and rooftops — measured during the three hottest months of the year, averaged across 2017–2024. LST is distinct from air temperature: it measures the thermal emission of the surface itself, not the ambient air at 1.5–2m height. Surface temperatures in densely built-up areas can exceed air temperatures by 10–20°C during heatwaves.
Why use it?
Extreme surface temperatures are a direct indicator of urban heat stress and its spatial distribution. Built surfaces such as asphalt and concrete absorb and retain solar radiation, generating the urban heat island effect and amplifying risk for outdoor workers, vulnerable populations, and poorly cooled housing. Mapping LST identifies which neighborhoods — typically dense, low-vegetation urban cores — experience the greatest heat burden, informing targeted greening interventions, cool surface programs, and heat action planning.
How is this made?
The Landsat 8 satellite’s thermal infrared band (Band 10, 10.6–11.2 µm) captures the thermal emission of the land surface. The pipeline uses Landsat 8 Collection 2, Level 2, Tier 1 imagery from Google Earth Engine (LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2), filtered to the three hottest months of the year for each year from 2017 to 2024. Cloud and saturation pixels are masked using the QA_PIXEL and QA_RADSAT bands. Monthly mean composites are computed for the seasonal window, then averaged across years. Values are converted from Kelvin to Celsius (subtracting 273.15 °C).
How should we interpret it?
High-value (hot) pixels correspond to surfaces with low evapotranspiration and high thermal mass: asphalt roads, rooftops, industrial areas, and sparse-vegetation zones. Low-value (cool) pixels typically correspond to vegetated areas, water bodies, and well-shaded spaces. Because LST measures surface temperature, not ambient thermal comfort, it should be used alongside humidity and wind data for a complete heat stress assessment. LST does not directly measure the urban heat island effect (which is defined by the temperature difference between urban and surrounding rural areas at night), but it serves as a strong spatial proxy for daytime heat concentration.
Under the hood
tasks/lst/collection.py builds a Landsat 8 collection filtered to the seasonal window via fns.Composite, applies cloud masking with maskL8sr(), and computes a seasonal mean composite using comp.seasonal('summer', 'mean'). The thermal band is scaled to Kelvin (multiply by 0.00341802, add 149.0) and converted to Celsius server-side before export via fns.tiled_collection() at 30m. The output is saved as {city}_lst_summer.tif. The LST map is rendered in R via core/R/ using the summer_lst layer definition in source/layers.yml.

What is it?
This map shows the density and health of vegetation using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). NDVI is derived from the near-infrared (NIR) and red spectral bands of Sentinel-2 imagery:
\[NDVI = \frac{NIR - Red}{NIR + Red}\]
Values range from −1 to 1. Pixels below 0.14 indicate water, rock, or artificial surfaces. Values of 0.14–0.18 represent very sparse or barren land; 0.18–0.27 correspond to shrub and grassland; 0.27–0.36 indicate sparse vegetation; and values above 0.36 indicate dense vegetation such as urban parks, forests, or mature crops. The map represents the seasonal (summer) median composite averaged over 2017–2024.
Why use it?
Vegetation distribution in cities has wide-ranging implications for health, climate resilience, and environmental quality. Urban green space reduces ambient temperature through evapotranspiration, providing a natural counterpart to LST hotspots. Vegetation helps absorb rainfall and reduce surface runoff, lowering flood risk downstream. Trees and shrubs also intercept and deposit particulate matter, providing passive air quality benefits. Beyond these environmental functions, green spaces support social wellbeing — they serve as gathering places and provide mental health benefits, a role that proved especially important during the COVID-19 pandemic.1 Comparing NDVI against LST identifies areas where targeted greening could deliver maximum cooling benefit.2
How is this made?
Sentinel-2 Harmonized imagery (COPERNICUS/S2_HARMONIZED) is filtered to scenes with less than 10% cloud cover for the summer season of each year (2017–2024). Cloud pixels are masked using the QA60 band. Median composites are computed per season, and NDVI is calculated server-side as (B8 − B4) / (B8 + B4), using Band 8 (NIR, 780–885 nm) and Band 4 (Red, 650–860 nm).3 Both bands have a native resolution of 10m. The resulting seasonal NDVI composite is exported at 10m and saved as {city}_ndvi_season.tif.
How should we interpret it?
NDVI captures both vegetation density and vegetation health at a given point in time. Because the map shows a seasonal median, it reflects peak-green conditions for summer — areas with seasonal deciduous vegetation may appear greener than their year-round average. NDVI does not distinguish between different vegetation types, so a dense urban park and a productive crop field with similar canopy structure would show similar values. NDVI also does not capture the social accessibility or quality of green spaces — high NDVI areas may be private gardens or industrial green buffers inaccessible to the public.
Under the hood
tasks/ndxi/collection.py builds a Sentinel-2 collection filtered to the seasonal window and cloud fraction threshold, applies the QA60-based cloud mask via maskS2clouds(), and computes the median seasonal composite. NDVI is computed server-side and exported via fns.tiled_collection() at 10m. The output is saved as {city}_ndvi_season.tif. The vegetation map is rendered in R via core/R/ using the vegetation layer definition in source/layers.yml, which applies fixed NDVI breakpoints.

What is it?
Two complementary maps of the city’s forest status. The forest cover map shows current tree cover — specifically, areas where at least 20% of a 30m×30m pixel was covered by tree canopy of 5 metres or more in 2000 and that has not been lost by 2023 (with gain areas from 2000–2012 included). The deforestation map shows the year that each forested pixel experienced tree cover loss (encoded as 1–24 for 2001–2024).
Why use it?
Forests provide a range of ecosystem services with direct implications for urban resilience: they regulate the local water cycle through evapotranspiration, reduce surface runoff and flood risk, stabilize soils on slopes and riverbanks, sequester carbon, and filter air pollutants. Tracking deforestation identifies where these services are being eroded and may signal expanding agricultural use, land clearing for urban development, or wildfire activity. At the peri-urban fringe, deforestation pressure often correlates with informal settlement expansion.
How is this made?
The Hansen et al. Global Forest Change dataset is produced at the University of Maryland using Landsat time-series imagery. Areas of vegetation are first detected using red and near-infrared bands, then filtered by height — pixels with ≥20% tree cover at ≥5m height are classified as forest. The dataset provides a 2000 baseline tree cover map plus annual layers of forest loss (2001–2024) and a 2000–2012 forest gain map. The City Scan pipeline derives two outputs: a current forest cover raster for approximately 2023 (starting from the 2000 baseline, subtracting loss through 2023, adding gain), and a deforestation year raster encoding when each loss pixel occurred.
How should we interpret it?
The forest cover map shows where trees currently exist, not whether the land is legally designated as forest. Urban parks and tree-lined streets with sufficient canopy density may appear as forested. The deforestation map reveals the spatial and temporal pattern of loss — clusters of loss in the same year may indicate clearing events or fire episodes; scattered annual loss may reflect gradual encroachment. As with all global remote sensing products, accuracy varies by forest type and canopy structure; tropical forests tend to have higher detection accuracy than sparse dryland woodlands.
Under the hood
tasks/forest/collection.py loads the Hansen GFC v1.12 image (UMD/hansen/global_forest_change_2024_v1_12) from Google Earth Engine. Current forest cover is derived as: forestCover2000 (≥20%) − lossThrough2023 + gain2000-2012 ≥ 1. The binary forest cover and the deforestation year (lossyear) bands are each exported via fns.tiled_collection() at 30m with nearest-neighbor resampling to preserve discrete values. Both rasters are saved as int8 and int16 respectively with nodata=0. Forest and deforestation maps are rendered in R via core/R/ using the forest and deforest layer definitions in source/layers.yml.

What is it?
A catalog of large flood events recorded by the Dartmouth Flood Observatory, filtered to events whose spatial extent intersects the city’s AOI. Each event includes start and end dates, the main cause, severity level, and figures for deaths and displaced persons. The chart shows the ten most significant events (ranked by a composite of deaths, displacement, and severity), with all others plotted but unlabelled.
Note that the death and displacement figures reflect the entire flood event’s geographic extent, which may be considerably larger than the city’s boundary.
Why use it?
Historical flood events ground-truth modeled hazard layers and reveal which types of flooding have most affected the city in the past. Repeated events in the same season or from the same cause (e.g., cyclone-driven rainfall) indicate recurring vulnerabilities that warrant priority attention.
How is this made?
The Dartmouth Flood Observatory archive is stored in a GCS bucket as a spatial file. The pipeline reads this archive, reprojects to the AOI’s CRS, validates geometries (repairing self-intersections where necessary), and filters for events intersecting the AOI. A severity-weighted score combining deaths, displacement, and the observatory’s severity rating is used to label the ten most significant events on the chart.
How should we interpret it?
Events are plotted on a timeline with point size or color encoding severity. The archive may not capture all significant local floods — it emphasizes events large enough to appear in international reporting, with a known bias toward events near settlements and roads.
Under the hood
tasks/flood_events/collection.R reads the Dartmouth archive spatial file from a GCS bucket, repairs any self-intersecting geometries with sf::st_make_valid() (switching off S2 spherical geometry temporarily to handle edge cases), and filters for events that spatially intersect the AOI. A severity-weighted score — computed as the product of normalized deaths, normalized displacement, and the observatory severity rating — ranks all events; the top 10 receive annotated text labels on the chart. The chart is rendered by tasks/flood_events/charts/index.qmd.

What is it?
There are 12 total flood hazard maps, covering three flood types and their combination, each overlaid with population density, built-up area, and social infrastructure layers. The flood types are:

Fluvial (riverine) flooding occurs when a watercourse overflows its banks due to high upstream flow — from intense rainfall, snowmelt, or dam releases. It can strike an area even during dry local conditions if the triggering event occurred upstream.
Pluvial (rainwater) flooding is floodwater that has not yet, or cannot, reach a watercourse. It occurs independently of overflowing water bodies and can affect any urban area, including elevated ones. Surface water flooding develops when drainage systems are overwhelmed; flash floods arrive faster than the drainage network can absorb, often from torrential local rainfall. Both are worsened by impervious urban surfaces that limit infiltration.1
Coastal flooding occurs when seawater inundates normally dry coastal land, typically via storm surge driven by severe winds coinciding with high tides. It can also result from tsunamis or from gradual sea level rise pushing tides above historic levels.

The combined flood zone represents the spatial union of all three types and is particularly relevant because flood types can compound — a coastal storm surge can impair drainage capacity, while a precipitation event may simultaneously cause both pluvial and fluvial flooding.
Why use it?
Urban density means that more people and assets are concentrated in flood-prone areas. Cities often occupy river confluences or coastal locations chosen for access to water, and impervious surfaces reduce natural infiltration, increasing runoff. Flooding causes immediate harm (death, injury), damage to buildings and infrastructure, economic disruption, environmental contamination, and displacement. Knowing the spatial pattern of flood exposure — disaggregated by flood type — enables targeted infrastructure investment, informed land-use planning, and preparation of non-structural responses such as early warning systems and evacuation plans.

What is it?
Two terrain maps derived from the FABDEM (Forest and Buildings Removed DEM): an elevation raster showing height above sea level and a slope raster showing terrain gradient in degrees. FABDEM is a bare-earth model that removes the vertical contribution of buildings and tree canopies from the Copernicus DEM, making it more suitable for hydrological and urban analysis than standard surface models.
Why use it?
Elevation and slope influence flood risk, landslide susceptibility, infrastructure cost, and service delivery. Low-lying areas are prone to pluvial or fluvial flooding; steep slopes increase landslide risk and make road construction more challenging. These two layers provide the terrain baseline that underpins many hazard analyses in this section.
How is this made?
FABDEM tiles are downloaded from a public GCS bucket and mosaicked for the AOI (falling back to the GEE community catalog, then USGS SRTM, if tiles are unavailable). The slope raster is derived by reprojecting the elevation raster to a local UTM CRS, computing the gradient with numpy.gradient, and converting to degrees via arctangent. The slope raster is then reprojected back to EPSG:4326 and clipped to the AOI.
How should we interpret it?
The elevation map identifies low-lying areas at potential flood risk and elevated areas that may serve as natural refuges. The slope map highlights zones where construction is constrained: slopes above 15–20° are challenging for dense development; slopes above 30° present significant landslide risk. Both maps are most informative when overlaid with flood hazard, landslide, or population layers.
Under the hood
tasks/elevation/collection.py downloads FABDEM ZIP archives from GCS, extracts tiles, and mosaics them with rasterio.merge. A buffered clip (500m buffer, {city}_elevation_buf.tif) is also produced for use by the slope task. tasks/slope/collection.py reads the buffered elevation, reprojects to UTM, computes slope with numpy.gradient, and reprojects back to EPSG:4326.

What is it?
A map of landslide susceptibility at ~1km resolution, classifying land into five levels (very low to very high). Landslides are the mass movement of rock or soil down a slope and can take many forms — falls, topples, flows, and spreads — triggered by heavy rainfall, liquefaction, excavation, or stream erosion. For a full typology, see the USGS Landslide Handbook.
Why use it?
Landslides can directly damage buildings and infrastructure in their path, and the secondary effects — blocked roads, broken pipes, downed power lines — can disrupt far larger areas. Road construction is a common trigger, as excavation and infill weaken slopes. Landslide susceptibility maps can direct new development away from high-risk zones and identify where slope stabilization or vegetation measures are warranted.
How is this made?
The model uses a fuzzy heuristic approach combining five globally available inputs: slope (from the Viewfinder Panoramas DEM, aggregated to the maximum 30-arc-second cell value), lithological class (reclassified from Bouysse’s Geological Map of the World into five strength levels), distance to fault lines, presence of OSM highway segments, and forest loss (from the Hansen dataset, 2000–2013). Non-slope variables are combined with a fuzzy gamma operator (γ = 0.9), then multiplied by the transformed slope variable to ensure flat terrain cannot receive high susceptibility scores. The resulting index is classified into five breakpoints (0.11, 0.49, 0.671, 0.75) so that each class covers roughly half the area of the previous one. The model achieves an AUC of 0.82 on the classified output, validated against 1,194 global landslide events.
The susceptibility formula is:
\(Susceptibility = \left(1 - \prod_{i}^{n} (1 - X_i)\right)^{0.9} \cdot \left( \prod_{i}^{n} X_i \right)^{0.1} \cdot S\)
where \(X_i\) is the transformed non-slope variable \(i\) and \(S\) is the transformed slope variable.2
How should we interpret it?
Susceptibility measures how prone a site is to landslide formation given its intrinsic properties — it does not indicate probability over a time period. The very high class covers approximately 3% of global land area and has a positive likelihood ratio about 100 times greater than the very low class. Because the model uses globally available data, it cannot capture fine-grained soil heterogeneity within grid cells, and does not differentiate between landslide types.
Under the hood
tasks/landslide/collection.py downloads the pre-classified landslide susceptibility GeoTIFF from a public GCS bucket and clips it to the AOI using rasterio.mask. tasks/landslide/analysis.py computes summary statistics (min, percentiles, mean) over the clipped raster. The susceptibility map and the built-up area overlay are rendered in R via core/R/ using the landslides layer definition in source/layers.yml. The built-up overlay is derived by masking the susceptibility raster to the WSF Evolution footprint.

What is it?
A scatter chart of significant earthquakes within 500km of the city, drawn from a merged catalog of the USGS FDSN (comprehensive, including small events) and the NOAA NCEI/WDS Global Significant Earthquake Database (curated, with damage and casualty metadata). Events appearing in both sources are deduplicated using a proximity and magnitude threshold. The NCEI database defines damage levels by monetary cost: limited (<$1M), moderate ($1–5M), severe ($5–24M), extreme ($25M+).
Why use it?
The earthquake catalog provides historical context for seismic activity in and around the city. Combined with the Seismic Hazard and Liquefaction maps, it helps establish whether past events have affected the city and at what magnitude and depth. Seismic risk in cities has grown largely due to urbanization, poor land-use planning, and inadequate building codes — understanding the historical record supports investment in retrofitting and preparedness.
How is this made?
The USGS API is queried for all earthquakes of magnitude ≥ 1.0 within a 500km radius of the city centroid, back to 1900. The NCEI API is queried for the same period globally and results are filtered spatially. Events are merged and deduplicated: events within 1 day, 50km, and 0.8 magnitude units of each other are treated as the same event, retaining the NCEI row (which carries richer damage metadata).
Under the hood
tasks/earthquake/collection.R queries the USGS FDSN REST API (earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query) and the NOAA NCEI Hazard Service API (ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/earthquakes) using the httr2 package, with paginated requests for the NCEI endpoint. The output CSV uses the NCEI column schema with NA values for USGS-only events. What is it?
A map showing where soils are most susceptible to liquefaction — the process by which strong earthquake vibrations temporarily convert water-saturated sediment into a fluid-like state, causing the ground to lose its load-bearing capacity. When liquefaction occurs, buildings and bridges can tilt or collapse, and gentle slopes can begin to flow. This map classifies susceptibility into five levels (very low to very high) based on soil and terrain characteristics, independent of any specific earthquake. Liquefaction is most commonly triggered by earthquakes, but non-seismic loads — such as dam failures and mine tailings impoundments — can also raise pore water pressure sufficiently to induce it.3
Why use it?
While seismic hazard is roughly uniform across a city’s area, liquefaction susceptibility varies considerably based on soil type, saturation, and drainage. Understanding which areas are more susceptible guides decisions on building codes, foundation design, and soil improvement. The three general responses are: avoiding susceptible areas, engineering more resistant foundations, and strengthening the soil through drainage, densification, or replacement.4
How is this made?
The Zhu et al. model uses geospatial regression trained on observed liquefaction (and non-liquefaction) from 27 earthquake events in six countries. The coastal model (within 20km of the sea) uses precipitation, distance to water bodies, and time-averaged shear wave velocity \(V_{S30}\) (approximated from slope); the inland model replaces distance to water bodies with water table depth. Because the trained model requires peak ground velocity (PGV) as an earthquake loading proxy, PGV is removed from the final susceptibility output to produce a site-characteristic rather than event-specific map. The resulting values are classified into five ordinal levels.
How should we interpret it?
Susceptibility differs from probability: susceptibility is a time-independent characteristic of the site, while probability would incorporate the likelihood of a triggering earthquake. High liquefaction susceptibility in a low-seismicity area does not mean liquefaction is likely — view this map alongside the Seismic Hazard map. The 1.2km resolution and the use of slope-derived \(V_{S30}\) (rather than in-situ measurements) mean that significant within-cell variation may exist.
Under the hood
tasks/liquefaction/collection.py downloads the pre-classified liquefaction susceptibility GeoTIFF from a public GCS bucket and clips it to the AOI using rasterio.mask. The output is a single-band raster with five ordinal class values. The susceptibility map and built-up area overlay are rendered in R via core/R/ using the liquefaction layer definition in source/layers.yml. The built-up overlay is derived by masking the susceptibility raster to the WSF Evolution footprint, consistent with the landslide built-up overlay.

What is it?
A map of Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) representing the seismic shaking intensity with a 10% probability of being exceeded in 50 years — corresponding to a ~475-year return period — on reference rock conditions (shear wave velocity 760–800 m/s). PGA is the standard metric for structural design and seismic risk assessments. An earthquake with moderate damage potential (PGA ~0.1–0.2g) can cause structural damage to unreinforced masonry and movement of wood-frame structures.
Why use it?
Seismic hazard is the foundation for understanding earthquake risk to people and assets. By itself it describes the shaking potential; combined with Liquefaction Susceptibility and building inventory data, it enables fuller risk assessment. Seismic risk in cities has grown primarily due to rapid urbanization, informal construction, and the concentration of population in poorly engineered buildings. This map provides the spatial baseline for prioritizing seismic retrofitting and resilient design standards.
How is this made?
The GEM hazard model is produced using OpenQuake, an open-source probabilistic seismic hazard analysis platform. It incorporates global seismicity catalogs, fault source models, and ground motion prediction equations. The 2023 version covers the globe at ~3 arc-minute resolution. The City Scan pipeline downloads and clips the v2023_1_pga_475_rock_3min.tif raster to the AOI.
How should we interpret it?
The map shows relative seismic shaking intensity across the city at the 475-year return period. Higher PGA values indicate areas with greater expected shaking — though at the ~5km resolution, the map is most useful for city-to-city comparison and broad zoning rather than site-specific structural design. Combine with the Liquefaction Susceptibility map to identify where shaking may be amplified by soil conditions.

What is it?
A map showing the relative importance of each road segment to the city’s overall road network, measured by edge betweenness centrality. Betweenness is the share of all shortest-path trips (between intersections) that pass through a given road segment. Higher percentages indicate segments whose obstruction would disrupt travel for a larger proportion of the city.
Why use it?
Road networks are critical for the movement of people and goods, emergency response, and evacuation. A non-critical street obstruction may affect only nearby residents; the obstruction of a highly critical segment during a flood or earthquake could broadly disrupt economic and social life and impede rescue operations. Identifying critical segments guides investment in resilience measures — elevating flood-exposed sections, adding redundant routes, or siting transit infrastructure on well-connected corridors.
How is this made?
The OSM road network is extracted for primary and secondary road types within the city AOI. The edge betweenness centrality algorithm maps the shortest path between all intersection pairs (or a 500-sample approximation for large cities, shown to produce similar results). Each segment’s betweenness score is expressed as the percentage of total trips using that segment. The road network and centrality values are saved to a GeoPackage for mapping.
How should we interpret it?
Cities with grid networks or many alternative routes show lower maximum betweenness scores — fewer segments are truly critical. Cities with radial or tree-like structures concentrate betweenness on a small number of segments. This analysis treats all road segments and intersections equally, which does not reflect capacity differences between, say, a motorway and a residential street. Trip distribution also differs from shortest-path logic in practice; congestion, preferences, and road quality all affect actual route choice.
Under the hood
tasks/accessibility/collection.py downloads the OSM road network graph via ox.graph_from_polygon() using OSMnx, with a 5km buffer around the AOI. The graph is saved as both a GeoPackage ({city}_nodes_and_edges.gpkg) and a GraphML file. tasks/accessibility/analysis.py computes edge and node betweenness centrality via nx.edge_betweenness_centrality() and nx.betweenness_centrality() from NetworkX, using a sample of 500 intersection nodes for large networks to keep computation tractable. Centrality values are joined back to the edges GeoDataFrame and saved to {city}_nodes_and_edges_centralities.gpkg. The road criticality and network maps are rendered in R via core/R/ using the roads and roads_network layer definitions in source/layers.yml.

What is it?
The Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI) measures moisture content in vegetation using Sentinel-2 near-infrared and shortwave infrared bands:
\[NDMI = \frac{NIR - SWIR}{NIR + SWIR}\]
This map shows the seasonal (summer) median NDMI composite averaged over 2017–2024. Negative values indicate water-stressed vegetation; positive values indicate well-watered or potentially waterlogged vegetation.
Why use it?
Moisture stress in vegetation affects agricultural productivity, ecosystem resilience, and wildfire risk. Areas with persistently low NDMI — particularly during dry seasons — are more susceptible to vegetation loss and combustion. NDMI is especially useful as a precursor indicator when combined with the Fire Weather Index and Burnability layers.
How is this made?
Sentinel-2 Harmonized imagery is filtered to scenes with less than 10% cloud cover for the summer season (2017–2024). Clouds are masked using the QA60 band. Median composites are computed per season and NDMI is calculated as (B8 − B11) / (B8 + B11), using Band 8 (NIR) and Band 11 (SWIR). The resulting composite is exported at 10m and saved as {city}_ndmi_season.tif.
How should we interpret it?
NDMI ranges from −1 to 1. Values below 0 indicate water stress; values approaching −1 represent severely stressed or bare land. Because the map shows a seasonal median, it reflects typical conditions during the hottest months — areas that are chronically dry will show consistently low values.
Under the hood
tasks/ndxi/collection.py handles both NDVI and NDMI, selecting the appropriate Sentinel-2 band pair via the INDEX_BANDS dictionary (ndmi uses B8 NIR and B11 SWIR). It builds a Sentinel-2 Harmonized collection filtered to the summer season and scenes with less than 10% cloud cover, applies the QA60-based cloud mask via maskS2clouds(), and computes the seasonal median composite server-side in GEE using fns.Composite. The NDMI composite is exported at 10m via fns.tiled_collection() and saved as {city}_ndmi_season.tif. The drought map is rendered in R via core/R/ using the drought layer definition in source/layers.yml.

A raster map showing the potential for combustion of each land area based on its land cover type. The 2020 ESA CCI land cover classification is reclassified into a burnability score from 0 to 1 using a mapping derived from global wildfire occurrence research. Dense closed forest receives the highest score (1.0); urban and permanent water bodies receive 0.
Why use it?
Burnability captures fuel availability — one of the three key components of wildfire risk alongside ignition sources and atmospheric conditions. Areas with high burnability scores that also experience high Fire Weather Index values or low NDMI represent zones of compounded wildfire potential. This is especially relevant at the urban-rural interface where vegetation encroaches on settled areas.
How is this made?
The ESA CCI 2020 land cover raster is downloaded from GCS and clipped to the AOI. Each pixel’s class code is mapped to a burnability score using the following scheme, based on Gannon et al. (2021) and historical MODIS wildfire intensity patterns:



Score

0.16

0.33

0.50

0.83

1.0

How should we interpret it?
The burnability score represents relative fuel load and ignition potential given the land cover type — it does not predict that a fire will occur. High-burnability areas near urban edges are most actionable for vegetation management and firebreak planning. Use alongside the FWI chart and Drought map for a fuller assessment of wildfire conditions.
Under the hood
tasks/landcover_burn/collection.py reads the ESA CCI 2020 land cover GeoTIFF (ESACCI.tif) from a GCS bucket via GDAL’s /vsigs/ virtual file system, clips it to the AOI using rasterio.mask, and reclassifies each pixel’s integer class code to a burnability float score using the CLASS_TO_BURN lookup dictionary. The reclassified raster is saved as {city}_burnable.tif. The burnability map is rendered in R via core/R/ using the burnable layer definition in source/layers.yml.

tasks/fwi/



What is it?
Two complementary fire risk indicators:

Historical Burnt Area: A map of fire event centroids from the GlobFire dataset, derived from MODIS MCD64A1 monthly burned area product. Each point represents a distinct fire event, showing where fires have historically occurred in and around the city.
Fire Weather Index (FWI): A seasonal chart of the weekly 95th-percentile FWI from NASA’s GEOS-5 atmospheric reanalysis (2016–2021). The FWI combines fuel moisture, wind, and buildup index into a single measure of wildfire potential. Values are categorized as Very Low (<5.2), Low (5.2–11.2), Moderate (11.2–21.3), High (21.3–38.0), Very High (38.0–50), and Extreme (>50).

Why use it?
Wildfires are becoming more frequent and destructive globally, with climate-driven increases in temperature and drought extending fire seasons. The historical fire map shows where burning has occurred, which may reflect recurring ignition sources (agricultural clearing, power lines, dry grasslands) or seasonal fire corridors. The FWI chart reveals which months have the highest atmospheric potential for wildfire — a critical complement to burnability and drought maps, since not all high-FWI days result in fires.
How is this made?
For burnt area, GlobFire FlatGeobuf files are downloaded from a public GCS bucket for each month from 2001 to 2020, filtered to a 1-degree buffer around the AOI. Fire event records are compiled into a GeoPackage and CSV.
For the FWI, NASA GEOS-5 daily FWI rasters are downloaded from GCS, clipped to the AOI, and a 95th-percentile value is extracted per week, then averaged across years to produce the seasonal FWI profile shown in the chart.
How should we interpret it?
The FWI is a relative index calibrated to local baseline conditions — months with higher values indicate relatively elevated fire weather risk. It captures atmospheric conditions only and does not account for vegetation availability, ignition sources, or fire management. FWI values must be interpreted locally: absolute values are not directly comparable between cities or regions. The historical fire map provides empirical grounding; the absence of fire events in a high-burnability area may reflect fire suppression, or simply that ignition conditions have not yet coincided with high fuel loads.
Under the hood
For burnt area, tasks/burned_area/collection.py iterates over year-month combinations from 2001 to 2020, reading monthly GlobFire FlatGeobuf files from a public GCS bucket (city-scan-global-public/globfire_fgb/). Each file is read with geopandas.read_file() filtered to a bounding box 1° around the AOI. All records are compiled into a GeoDataFrame, saved as {city}_globfire_centroids.gpkg and a CSV equivalent. The burnt area map is rendered in R via core/R/.
For the FWI, tasks/fwi/collection.py downloads daily NASA GEOS-5 FWI GeoTIFFs from GCS for the configured year range via GDAL /vsicurl/, clips each to the AOI, and assembles a dictionary keyed by date string. tasks/fwi/analysis.py stacks all daily rasters along the time axis and computes a per-pixel 98.6th-percentile summary raster (generate_nth_raster()), plus a weekly 95th-percentile time series (compute_weekly_percentiles()). The seasonal FWI chart is rendered by tasks/fwi/charts/index.qmd with FWI risk category bands (Very Low through Extreme) as background shading.

All other invocations proceed to scan initialization.

17.2 2. Scan initialization
After flag parsing, main() instantiates Scan (defined in core/config/scan.py). The Scan object is the city context — it carries directory paths, city metadata, and loaded config — and is passed into every subsequent step.
Scan.__init__() runs in this order:

Resolve scan ID

If --scan-id was given → uses mnt/<scan_id>/01-user-input/ as the input source
Otherwise → calls scan_init(), which searches mnt/ for folders matching the {country}-{city} suffix, then either prompts [e]xisting / [n]ew (interactive) or auto-creates (non-TTY or -e flag)
Scan ID format: YYYY-MM-{country}-{city} for single-country, YYYY-MM-{city} for multi-country AOIs

Load city config — reads city_inputs.yml → sets city_name, first_year, last_year, flood_threshold, flood_year, flood_ssp, flood_return_periods, fwi_first_year, fwi_last_year, and other city parameters
Load AOI — reads the boundary shapefile from 01-user-input/AOI/
Resolve country — calls find_country() (core/py/aoi_module.py) which intersects the AOI against a country boundaries dataset → sets country_iso3, country_name, country_iso3_list, multi_country
Create output directories
mnt/<scan_id>/
├── 02-process-output/spatial/
├── 02-process-output/tabular/
├── 03-render-output/maps/
└── 03-render-output/plots/
Sync project files — calls sync_project_files() (core/config/sync.py), skipped if --keep or render-only mode
Load runtime config — reads menu.yml → scan.menu; reads source/layers.yml → scan.sources


17.2.1 File sync decision logic
On each run (unless --keep), the pipeline decides what code to copy into the city folder:
--sync targets given explicitly   →  copy only those targets
no project files in city folder   →  copy all four (first run)
non-interactive / no TTY          →  tasks only
interactive prompt:
  [t]  tasks only
  [o]  override all  (01-user-input/ is never touched)
  [k]  keep as-is
  [a]  abort
Sync targets: tasks/, core/, source/, scan-calculations/. A .here marker file is also written so R’s here package resolves paths correctly.

title: 17  Orchestration & Dependency Flow
text:
17.4 4. Authentication
Before executing tasks, main() checks whether any task in the run requires GEE or GCS access (using GEE_TASKS and GCS_TASKS sets read from source/tasks.yml) and initializes credentials accordingly.
GEE tasks (elevation, forest, landcover, lst, green, ndmi, nightlight, water_risk): Calls init_gee() in core/config/auth.py, which tries credentials in this order:
1. Cloud Run service account  (K_SERVICE env var present)
2. GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS  (env var pointing to a key file)
3. local gcloud ADC  (gcloud auth application-default login)
→ fail-fast with message: run `scan --check gee`
GCS tasks (wsf, fathom, landcover_burn, basic_info, oxford, coastal_erosion, sea_level_rise, elevation): Calls init_gcs(), which verifies that ADC credentials exist and sets GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS so GDAL can read from /vsigs/ paths.

title: 17  Orchestration & Dependency Flow
text:
17.5 5. Task execution

17.5.1 Serial mode (default)
for task_name in topo_sorted_tasks:
    result = run_task(task_name, scan, step)   # core/config/run.py
    if --upload:
        upload_task_outputs(scan, task_name, step, ...)
Each task is exception-isolated — a failure in one task is caught and logged, and execution continues with the next task.


17.5.2 Parallel mode (--parallel)
Calls run_parallel() in core/config/multitask.py:

Each task runs in its own thread
Concurrency is semaphore-gated per resource type: separate semaphores for GEE, GCS, and OSM prevent rate-limit collisions
A live TUI shows per-task status and lets you stream a task’s log to the screen by pressing its key
--auto-exit skips the “press any key to exit” pause; this flag is auto-injected when --multicity --parallel is combined to prevent blocking between cities



17.5.3 Inside run_task() (core/config/run.py)

Imports the task module: importlib.import_module(module_path)
Wraps each phase in ErrorTracker() — captures status (OK / WARNING / ERROR / NO_DATA) and any messages
Dispatches based on step:








step value
What runs




None (default)
collect then analyze in sequence


"collect"
collect phase only


"analyze"
analyze phase only


"multianalysis"
multianalysis.R or .py via subprocess; output streamed live; any “Error” string triggers WARN status


"charts"
quarto render tasks/<task>/charts/index.qmd




Returns {phase: status, _messages: {...}, _source: "..."} — the source label comes from scan.sources[task_name]



17.5.4 Render path (--render)
Render targets run via subprocess after task execution (or standalone):



Target
Command




maps
Rscript core/R/maps-static.R


scan-calculations
quarto render scan-calculations/


charts <task>
quarto render tasks/<task>/charts/index.qmd

title: 17  Orchestration & Dependency Flow
text:
17.6 6. Outputs
All outputs land under the city folder in mnt/:
mnt/<scan_id>/
├── 02-process-output/
│   ├── spatial/     ← rasters and vector files from collect / analyze
│   └── tabular/     ← CSVs and statistics from analyze
└── 03-render-output/
    ├── maps/        ← static map PNGs from --render maps
    └── plots/       ← chart PNGs from --render charts / scan-calculations
A run summary is also appended to logs/task_report.txt:
task | step | status | source | message | timestamp

title: 17  Orchestration & Dependency Flow
text:
17.7 Multi-city batch mode
--multicity is an early-exit path that runs the entire pipeline once per city by spawning subprocesses. run_multicity() in core/config/run.py:

Reads inputs/multi_inputs.yml
Resolves city list — two modes (combinable):

multipolygon: reads a GeoDataFrame; auto-extracts each row as a city AOI shapefile to inputs/AOI/{city_slug}/
cities list: uses pre-made AOI folders already present in inputs/AOI/

For each city:

Calls scan_init() to get or create the scan ID
Calls prepare_inputs() to write city_inputs.yml into the city’s input folder
Spawns: python -m tasks --scan-id <id> <passthrough_args>
Passthrough args = all original args except --multicity

If --parallel is in passthrough args and --auto-exit is absent, --auto-exit is injected automatically to prevent the TUI from blocking between cities

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.1 Git Branching System
We welcome contributions to City Scan, from new data layers to documentation improvements.
This document explains how to add new analytical modules to the tasks framework and integrate them into the pipeline.
This project follows a modular, reproducible, and readable design philosophy. Each task module represents one analytical domain (e.g. air quality, population, hazard, etc.).
Before you start, let’s ensure we are on the same page on the branching system. This is to avoid pushing unstable updates to main.

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.1.1 Our Branching Model
main          → stable / production-like
  │
  └── unified   → This is where our initiative lives
         │
         ├── unified_alice
         ├── unified_bob
         ├── unified_issue_19
         └── unified_charlie
No one touches main directly.
No one pushes to unified without review.



20.1.2 What Contributors Do

Step 1 — Sync with remote
git fetch origin
git checkout unified
git pull


Step 2 — Create their personal branch
git checkout -b unified_alice
Naming convention:
unified_<name>
# or
unified_<issue>



Step 3 — Work normally
When you make updates to your code, commit locally:
git add .
git commit -m "Implement accessibility data parser"


Step 4 — Push their branch
git push -u origin unified_alice


Step 5 — Open a Pull Request
On GitHub / GitLab:
FROM: unified_alice
TO:   unified
Someone will review your code.




20.1.3 Safety Rules



Rule
Why




No direct commits to main
Prevent breaking prod


No direct commits to unified
Forces review


Always branch from unified
Prevents divergence


Small PRs
Easier review


One feature per branch
No tangled work

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.2 Task Architecture
Each task module lives in its own folder under tasks/ and follows this standard structure:
tasks/
└── <task_name>/
    ├── __init__.py          # registers collect(), analyze() entry points
    ├── collection.py        # downloads and clips data to AOI  (.py or .R)
    ├── analysis.py          # computes statistics and generates outputs  (.py or .R)
    ├── maps.yml             # [optional] map layers this task contributes
    ├── multianalysis.R      # [optional] cross-task R post-processing
    └── charts/              # [optional] Quarto charts for the scan report
        ├── _quarto.yml
        └── index.qmd
Example:
tasks/air_quality/
Reference implementation: tasks/air_quality

20.2.1 File Responsibilities







File
Responsibility




collection.py
Download / load raw data (cloud storage, API, direct download, etc.) and clip to AOI


analysis.py
Perform numerical / statistical / spatial analysis; write CSVs and spatial files


maps.yml
Declare which map layers this task contributes and any custom map-render scripts


charts/index.qmd
Quarto charts rendered into the combined scan report


multianalysis.R
Cross-task post-processing that depends on outputs from other tasks


__init__.py
Module registration — exposes collect() and analyze() entry points



Both collection.py and analysis.py may be Python or R scripts; the pipeline dispatches accordingly.

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.3 Linking a New Module to __main__.py
Each collect() and analyze() function is registered in tasks/{task_name}/__init__.py. All task modules are then discovered automatically at startup by tasks/__main__.py, which scans tasks/ for subdirectories containing an __init__.py.
To integrate a new module:

Implement collection.py and analysis.py inside your task folder
Expose collect() and analyze() in __init__.py
Register the task in source/tasks.yml (auth requirements, aliases, dependencies)

The two-phase pipeline must be preserved:

Collection → Analysis

Visualization (maps and charts) is handled separately via maps.yml / charts/ and rendered with --render maps or --render scan-calculations.

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.4 Function Design Rules

20.4.1 Required Function Signatures
All Python modules must use these standard arguments:







Parameter
Purpose




city_name: str
City identifier


output_dir: str
Root output directory (mnt/<scan_id>/)


aoi: GeoDataFrame
Area of interest geometry


return_* flags
Enable standalone testing without full pipeline



R scripts receive equivalent values via core/R/setup.R, which loads the AOI, sets directory paths, and initialises shared packages.
This ensures consistent orchestration across both Python and R tasks.

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.5 Documentation & Style Guide

20.5.1 Docstrings
Every public function must include a NumPy-style docstring:
def compute_stats(...):
    """
   Summary of what this function is about.

    Parameters
    ----------
    what are the inputs to this function
    ...
    Returns
    -------
    what are the outputs of this function
    ...
    """


20.5.2 Logging
Use the shared logger:
from utils.log_module import setup_logger
logger = setup_logger(__name__)
Never use print() for operational logging.


20.5.3 Error Handling

Validate inputs at the start of each function
Log failures with logger.error(...)
Return None on failure instead of crashing the pipeline



20.5.4 Modularity & Readability

One responsibility per function
No hidden side effects
Avoid hard-coded paths — always use output_dir
Favor explicitness over cleverness

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.6 Standalone Testing
Every file should support standalone execution:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # minimal test example
This allows rapid local testing without running the full pipeline.

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.7 Folder Naming & Structure
Use snake_case for module names:
flood_event
ghs_builtup
elevation
After creating your folder, register the task in source/tasks.yml. This is where auth requirements (gee, gcs), CLI aliases, and inter-task dependencies are declared. The pipeline discovers tasks automatically by scanning tasks/ for subdirectories with an __init__.py, but source/tasks.yml controls how they behave at runtime.

title: 20  Contributing
text:
20.8 Design Philosophy
This framework is designed for:

reproducibility
scientific transparency
easy extension
clear audit trails

Every contribution should preserve these goals.

22.1 Prerequisites
A step-by-step guide for team members who want to update or extend this technical reference. Covers the editing workflow, branch conventions, and how to publish changes to GitHub Pages.

title: 22  Editing This Reference

title: 22  Editing This Reference
text:
22.2 Repository Structure
Documentation lives in the docs/ folder of the main city-scan repository. Each page is a Quarto Markdown file (.qmd):
city-scan/
└── docs/
    ├── _quarto.yml         # book structure and settings
    ├── index.qmd           # landing page
    ├── *.qmd               # one file per chapter
    ├── references.bib      # bibliography
    └── image/              # shared images
The compiled website is published to the gh-pages branch and served at https://cityresilience.github.io/city-scan/.

title: 22  Editing This Reference
text:
22.3 Editing Workflow

22.3.1 1. Switch to new_docs
All documentation edits happen on new_docs — never commit directly to main or gh-pages.
git checkout new_docs
git pull origin new_docs      # always pull latest before editing


22.3.2 2. Edit .qmd files
Open the relevant .qmd file in docs/ and edit it. Quarto Markdown is standard Markdown with optional callouts, cross-references, code blocks, and diagrams.
To preview changes live in your browser:
cd docs
quarto preview
This starts a local server (usually at http://localhost:4848) that hot-reloads as you save.


22.3.3 3. Add a new page (optional)

Create a new .qmd file in docs/, e.g. docs/my-new-page.qmd
Start the file with an H1 heading: # My New Page
Register it in docs/_quarto.yml under the appropriate part: section:

- part: "Collaborating"
  chapters:
    - editing-this-reference.qmd
    - my-new-page.qmd


22.3.4 4. Commit and push to new_docs
# Stage only docs source files — never stage docs/_book/
git add docs/my-new-page.qmd docs/_quarto.yml
git commit -m "docs: add page on <topic>"
git push origin new_docs






Warning



Do not stage or commit anything inside docs/_book/. That folder contains compiled site output and is excluded by docs/.gitignore. Committing it to new_docs will bloat the repository with binary files.

title: 22  Editing This Reference
text:
22.4 Publishing Workflow
Once edits are committed to new_docs, publish to GitHub Pages from the docs/ directory:
cd docs
quarto publish gh-pages
Quarto will:

Re-render only changed pages (freeze: true skips unchanged code outputs)
Commit the compiled site to the local gh-pages branch
Push gh-pages to origin — GitHub Pages auto-deploys within ~1 minute

When prompted:
Update site at https://cityresilience.github.io/city-scan/? (Y/n)
Type Y and press Enter.






Note



First-time setup on a new machine: If you get an HTTP 400 error during the push step, run this once from the repo root, then re-publish:
git config http.postBuffer 524288000
This increases the git push buffer to 500 MB, which is needed for the initial upload of all site assets.

title: 22  Editing This Reference
text:
22.5 Branch Overview








Branch
Purpose
Who touches it




main
Stable code and configuration
Maintainers via PR


new_docs
Documentation source (.qmd files)
Editors directly


gh-pages
Compiled website — managed by Quarto
Never edit manually

title: 22  Editing This Reference
text:
22.6 Quick Reference
# Pull latest docs before editing
git checkout new_docs && git pull origin new_docs

# Start local preview
cd docs && quarto preview

# Commit documentation edits (from repo root)
git add docs/<changed-files>
git commit -m "docs: <short description>"
git push origin new_docs

# Publish to GitHub Pages (from docs/)
cd docs && quarto publish gh-pages

For reporting content issues or suggesting structural changes, see Reporting Issues. For contributing to the codebase itself, see Contributing.
